Rustic Maps SDK

Rustic Maps SDK

Rustic Maps SDK draws maps, resolves places, plans routes, follows a turn-by-turn trip, and routes offline. One Rust core serves Android (Kotlin), iOS (Swift), React Native (TypeScript), and WebAssembly (TypeScript) through one UniFFI contract. Map platforms connect through vendor-neutral provider contracts: MapQuest implements the platform API set, and any {z}/{x}/{y} raster or vector source connects through the URL-template providers.

Open the live wasm demo Run the apps on a hosted device Start building Downloads

What you get

One contract, four platforms

You call the same members on every target: Kotlin suspend functions, Swift async throwing methods, React Native promises, and the WebAssembly TypeScript surface. One UniFFI interface definition generates the native bindings, and the browser mirror is checked against it. The contract changes addition-only: existing members keep their signature and meaning.

Search, routing, and traffic

Ten provider contracts cover geocoding (forward and reverse), routing, the distance matrix, place search, traffic incidents, traffic flow, elevation, raster tiles, vector tiles, and offline routing. MapQuest implements geocoding, routing, the distance matrix, place search, traffic, and raster tiles with a shared rate limiter and bounded retries. The SDK adds a disk response cache with per-category time-to-live. URL-template providers serve any raster or vector base map.

A rendering core that draws anywhere

The renderer spans web-mercator projection, an anchored camera with animations and fit-bounds framing, exact frustum tile listing, a frame-driven tile scheduler with per-frame budgets and parent fallback, and a byte-budget tile texture pool feeding a wgpu pipeline. Raster and vector scenes draw on Android, iOS, and React Native surfaces and in the browser through WebGPU.

Turn-by-turn navigation

The navigation state machine follows the Ferrostar model. It composes banner and spoken instructions from the provider’s text, publishes speech triggers at documented distance bands, and leaves deviation handling and reroute policy at clear seams.

Offline maps

An OpenStreetMap PBF extract compiles into a compact, self-describing routing archive. An offline provider answers routes over the memory-mapped graph with recorded turn restrictions, and a fallback decorator wraps your online provider when you choose to fall back.

Structured diagnostics

A bounded, per-subsystem diagnostics ring streams structured log events to a listener with coordinate scrubbing at the sink. Readbacks expose frame tile statistics, cache terms, and provider-failure records, so a screen in your product can show what the SDK is doing.

The full call surface is the FFI contract; each member’s documentation lives in the generated API reference.

Requirements at a glance

  • Android: API level 24 or higher. The bindings AAR measures 16 MiB across three ABIs (8.7 to 13 MiB each after strip).
  • iOS: iOS 17 or higher. The XCFramework ships two arm64 slices.
  • React Native: React Native 0.88 or newer and React 19 or newer. The package ships as a source TurboModule and builds the native payload in your project unless you pack a prebuilt payload into the tarball.
  • WebAssembly: a browser with WebGPU. The wasm package measures 3.6 MiB.

Artifacts are distributed from the Downloads page rather than a package registry. Per-platform tables, artifact sizes, and the version policy are in Requirements and distributions.

Requirements and distributions

The SDK ships as release archives that you download and install into your project. This page lists the minimum platform versions, the artifact each platform installs, and what each artifact weighs. Downloads lists the released files and their checksums.

Android

Coroutinesorg.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core:1.10.2

The release ships two AARs:

  • rustic-maps-sdk-android-v0.1.0.aar — the Kotlin bindings and the Rust library for arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, and x86_64. The bindings AAR measures 16 MiB; its stripped libraries measure 12 MiB for arm64-v8a, 8.7 MiB for armeabi-v7a, and 13 MiB for x86_64.
  • rustic-maps-sdk-android-ui-v0.1.0.aar — the MapView and its Compose wrapper. It depends on the bindings AAR, so add both.

iOS

RequirementValue
Deployment targetiOS 17 or higher
Swift toolingswift-tools-version: 5.10 (Swift 5 language mode)
Architecturesarm64 (device) and arm64 (simulator)

The artifact is rustic-maps-sdk-ios-v0.1.0.xcframework.zip: the XCFramework containing the static library, its headers, and module maps, packaged for a Swift Package Manager binary target. Each slice measures 217 MiB, and 207 MiB after strip -x. A static archive carries every compiled object, and your final link discards unused code, so these archive sizes are not the size your application adds.

React Native

The artifact is rustic-maps-sdk-rn-v0.1.0.tgz, the TurboModule source package (@angoratek/rustic-maps-sdk). It carries the generated TypeScript surface, the JSI C++ glue, and the podspec and CMake wiring.

  • React Native and React versions. The generated glue targets React Native 0.88 or later and React 19 or later. For another version, regenerate the glue with a matching generator version.
  • Source package. The compiled native payload is optional. With it, the package installs ready to run. Without it, your project builds the Rust code on the first build.

WebAssembly

The wasm artifacts are:

  • rustic-maps-sdk-web-v0.1.0.tar.gz — the wasm module, its JavaScript shim, and both type files.
  • rustic-maps-sdk-web-v0.1.0.tgz — the same module with the npm manifest, licenses, and notices.

The package downloads 3.6 MiB, of which the wasm module is 3.4 MiB.

The browser surface renders through WebGPU. Chromium-based browsers support it flag-free since 113 (2023), Safari from version 26, and Firefox since 141 with desktop first. WebGPU is a secure-context API, so serve your page over HTTPS or from localhost, and test for navigator.gpu rather than sniffing the user agent. MDN’s WebGPU page carries the live compatibility table.

Notices

rustic-maps-sdk-notices-v0.1.0.md carries the third-party dependency notices that accompany your own distribution.

Versions policy

  • Pin exact versions. Release archives are immutable and carry a version in the file name, for example rustic-maps-sdk-android-v0.1.0.aar. Keep the version you validated against, and upgrade deliberately.
  • One version line. The Cargo workspace version is the single source of truth: the Android Maven publication, the npm packages, and the Swift manifest are all stamped from it at release time. The compiled SDK also returns its version through getSdkCompiledVersion across the FFI, so your diagnostics screen can verify the loaded library matches the artifacts you shipped.
  • The FFI contract changes addition-only. Existing members keep their signature and meaning, so a minor-version upgrade keeps your compiled bindings valid. Packaging changes, such as an artifact-set change or a renamed target, bump the minor version while the release is 0.x.
  • Semantic versioning from 0.1.0. A vX.Y.Z tag triggers a release. Tags are never moved, and a broken release is superseded by a new tag.
  • Checksums and signatures. Every release carries a per-asset SHA-256 checksum, an aggregated checksum manifest, and Sigstore signature bundles. Verifying them is part of the Downloads flow.

The sizes above are measured from the 0.1.0 artifacts.

Performance and profiling

This page is integration guidance: the practices that keep map rendering, routing, and navigation responsive, and the readbacks the SDK exposes so you can measure your own integration on your own hardware and scenes.

Measured on this machine

The browser frame has a committed, reproducible measurement. On an Apple Silicon host (GPUAdapter.info: apple · metal-3) with hardware WebGPU, a 1920 × 1080 vector base over the recorded demo tiles and a four-second pan, renderFrame costs 1.9 ms at the median and 2.2 ms at p95; every one of 120 measured frames stayed inside the 16.7 ms 60 Hz budget. The p99 sample (11.6 ms) is the frame that re-tessellates the overlay layer, not the steady state. The raster base over the same ground costs 0.1 ms at the median.

# from platform/web
node perf/run-frame-budget.mjs            # vector base
node perf/run-frame-budget.mjs --layer raster

The runner launches the host’s own Chromium with hardware WebGPU and prints the machine, adapter, scenario and per-stage distributions. Treat the table above as a starting point for your own measurement, not a guarantee: quote figures from your own device, power state and route mix.

Construct the SDK once

  • Build one MapSdk object and register your providers once at startup. Re-registration replaces every slot (including a cached tile slot), so an accidental double registration silently reopens the cache and resets its tuning: register, then tune with setRasterTileCacheTimeToLive.
  • Keep a single Navigator around the lifetime of a trip screen; subscriptions are explicit and cheap, but re-subscribing listeners is wasted work on every frame.

Frame the camera with the contract’s helpers

  • Prefer the fit_bounds camera constructor for route previews and search-result framing. It computes a top-down, north-up camera that keeps the whole box visible inside the insets you give it, instead of a hand-tuned zoom level that breaks on another screen size.
  • Give it real insets. Route cards, attribution, and sheets are overlays your application owns; the insets tell the camera what the map may not hide. The insets-aware framing is what keeps the destination inside the visible region on every device.
  • Read the camera back with the attribute getters (center, zoomLevel, bearingDegrees, pitchDegrees) when you need to persist or compare a pose; the camera carries no setters, so a new pose is a new constructor call.

Let the render loop stay explicit

  • Frames are explicit by design: the platform view drives draw from its own cadence (a display link or choreographer callback). Do not add a second render loop; serialize draws and never call draw again while a previous call is still in flight — a draw in flight reports the next frame busy, and the cadence retries it.
  • Poll isFrameSettled in the render pump to skip draw when a re-draw would present the same pixels: true when the camera, overlay list, and location indicator are unchanged and no pending tile pixels remain. This keeps battery cost near zero on a static map.
  • Read FrameStatistics from every draw. The four readiness counts (present, fallback, deferred, unavailable) always add up to the requested count, so a persistent slice of deferred tells you your per-frame fetch budget is the limiter on your network, and a slice of unavailable points at provider refusals rather than slow ones.
  • Feed gesture deltas through the SDK’s camera seam (pan by pixels, focal-point zoom and rotation) instead of moving the viewport yourself; the SDK clamps zoom and pitch through the camera’s own ranges and holds the focal point exactly.

Size the tile cache deliberately

  • Register the tile cache with an absolute byte budget that fits your product (the reference application’s demo budget is 16 MiB for the whole bundled demo region). The budget is a registration-time fact: retuning it means re-registering.
  • Set the tile time-to-live live through setRasterTileCacheTimeToLive. Imagery-provider terms put a ceiling on what the cache may retain; a request above the ceiling is accepted and the ceiling clamps what is stored. Read rasterTileCacheTerms to display the effective value, the ceiling, and the default in a settings or diagnostics screen.
  • Do not set a zero time-to-live; the call is refused because it would expire every entry on capture.

Keep the provider path under your quota

  • The provider implementation carries a shared token-bucket rate limiter and bounded idempotent retries. Treat RateLimitExhausted as “retry after the next refill”, not as an error to surface in the UI.
  • Cache-then-network is the default shape of every provider call, so repeated identical requests inside the time-to-live cost no quota. The tile category defaults to a 30-day time-to-live, the imagery terms ceiling.
  • Batch what the contracts batch: the distance matrix answers every origin-destination pair in one call; fetching matrix cells one by one multiplies your request count for the same data.

Use offline where it pays

  • The offline routing provider answers routes over a memory-mapped archive with A*; no network round trip. Compile an extract sized to the region your users drive in, not the planet: the compiler is deterministic and the archive is self-describing.
  • The offline routing decorator retries over the offline graph when the online provider fails, so a coverage-limited archive is a graceful degradation, not a failure mode. You wire it around your online provider; the SDK registers no fallback on your behalf. Its maneuver texts stay honest where the archive carries no street names.

Profile with the SDK’s own readbacks

  • Subscribe to diagnostics events at Info severity (or Debug for frame-path detail). Events stream fire-and-forget from bounded ring buffers, coordinates are scrubbed at the sink, and a slow listener can never slow the SDK.
  • Drain the backlog with the bounded flush readback from a non-frame context: the flush is synchronous and must stay out of the render path.
  • For provider failures, read latestProviderFailureDiagnostics after a suspicious session; the ring carries the contract, method, timestamp, and verbatim failure text for every failed foreign-callback provider call.
  • Measure on your target device and your real scenes. The SDK reports what it did (tile counts, frame statistics, cache terms, and the frame’s own stage spans in the browser), so a slow frame can be attributed to geometry, encoding or submission instead of guessed at.
  • In the browser, the frame never blocks on the network: missing tiles are fetched on their own tasks and the frame draws what it already holds. A page that renders on demand should listen for the canvas’s map-tile-arrived event and draw again, which is what the live demo page does.

Live demo

Open the live wasm demo

Try the SDK in your browser: pan and zoom a rendered map, plan a recorded route, follow a simulated trip with turn-by-turn guidance, and route over a compiled archive. The demo runs the same WebAssembly module the package ships, draws on a WebGPU canvas, and works without a provider key.

What the demo needs in a browser

  • WebGPU. Chromium-based browsers support it flag-free since 113. Safari ships it from version 26, and Firefox since 141 with desktop first. MDN’s WebGPU page carries the live compatibility table.
  • A secure context. The browser enables WebGPU only over HTTPS or localhost.
  • A runtime key for live calls. Keyless, the demo renders recorded tiles, plans recorded routes, drives the simulated trip, and serves offline routes. Open Settings from the gear in the panel header to apply a MapQuest key for live geocoding, routing, and tiles. The key stays in the page’s memory and is never persisted.

Run the same loop locally

Every guide in this book has a WebAssembly tab that uses the same surface. Install the wasm package and follow Your first map for the whole loop.

Mobile demo

Open the mobile demo

Run the Android, iOS, and React Native reference applications on a hosted device. Choose a platform and press Start demo; the session opens in its own browser tab for three minutes.

What the session is

The builds are the same reference applications the guides walk through: the map view, search and route planning, turn-by-turn simulation, the offline card, and the settings sheet. The hosted build may carry a dedicated provider credential issued for this demo alone. No visitor credential is involved, and the packages you download or install never carry one.

If a build cannot create a rendering surface on the hosted device, the app shows its own failure state instead of a blank frame.

The monthly budget

The demo runs on a free plan with 30 streamed minutes a month, shared by every visitor. Nothing streams until you press Start, and a session lasts three minutes. When the month’s minutes are gone, the page says so and the demo rests until the month turns over.

The daily limit

Each visitor gets a limited number of sessions per day. When you have used today’s sessions, the page asks you to come back tomorrow. The daily limit keeps one visitor from spending the shared monthly budget.

Developer quickstart

Build a map, resolve places, plan a route, and follow a guided trip. The same calls exist on Android (Kotlin), iOS (Swift), React Native (TypeScript), and WebAssembly (TypeScript) because all four bind one UniFFI contract. This page gives the order to do it in and the concepts the calls use. Each step links to the guide that shows it in full.

What you need

  • The SDK artifact for your platform, built or installed by Your first map.
  • A provider credential for search, routing, and traffic. A raster or vector base map from a URL-template source needs no credential.
  • The minimum platform version for your target: Android API 24, iOS 17, React Native 0.88, or a browser with WebGPU. Requirements and distributions lists the exact toolchains and artifact sizes.

What the SDK gives you

CallWhat it gives you
MapViewThe map surface. The shipped widget owns the platform surface, frame pump, gestures, and lifecycle. On WebAssembly you supply a canvas and render a frame on request.
setCameraCenter, zoom, bearing, and pitch. Zoom is continuous; pitch tops out at 75°.
setOverlaysRoute polylines, filled rings, point markers, A/B pins, and traffic flow, all in geographic coordinates.
forwardGeocode, suggest, searchProvider geocoding and place search. Results carry a coordinate.
calculateRouteA route with legs, steps, shapes, and instructions. Flatten the step shapes and you have the polyline.
startNavigation and location updatesA reducer that advances steps, grades deviation, and reports progress.
setVectorTileSourceA styled vector base map from any {z}/{x}/{y} vector source.
setProviderCredentialWithTileCache, offlineRouteFromArchiveBytesA disk tile cache with per-category time-to-live, and routes over an offline graph compiled from OpenStreetMap.

Set up in order

  1. Install the artifact. Build the package for your platform or download a release, then add it to your project. Your first map has the exact steps for Android, iOS, React Native, and WebAssembly.
  2. Create the SDK and register a provider. MapSdk starts with no providers. Apply a credential with setProviderCredential, or register a URL-template base map. Calls into an unregistered contract throw ProviderNotConfigured.
  3. Open the map and set the camera. Give the map view an SDK instance and a camera pose. The shared demo camera is Capitol Park, Sacramento at zoom 12, north-up and top-down.
  4. Add what you want to show. Overlays are geographic coordinates plus style. A calculated route’s step shapes flattened into one list make a route polyline.
  5. Plan and follow. Call calculateRoute, then deliver location updates to the Navigator. The reducer reports the active step, the distance remaining, and when a fix is off route.

Positions and the world square

A position is a GeographicCoordinate: latitude and longitude in decimal degrees on the WGS 84 ellipsoid. A region is a BoundingBox between a south-west and a north-east corner. A box never spans the antimeridian; encode a region that crosses it as two adjacent boxes.

The renderer does not draw latitude and longitude directly. Every coordinate is projected into the Web Mercator world square, where each position becomes two numbers in [0, 1]. The projection stops at about 85.05° north and south, so a coordinate near a pole sits on the square’s edge.

Tiles and zoom

A tile is one payload at one zoom level. Its address is a TileKey: a column, a row counted from the north, and the zoom level. At zoom 0 the world is one tile; each level doubles the columns and rows, so level z has 2^z of each.

A camera’s zoom is continuous from 0 through 24, and each unit doubles the on-screen scale. The tile grid changes only at whole levels, so the camera answers two questions: tileZoomLevel gives the nearest whole level for a tile fetch, and visibleTileKeys lists every tile at a chosen level that intersects the visible ground, sorted row-major from the north.

Cameras

A MapCamera is an immutable pose made of four values: center, zoom, bearing, and pitch. A new pose is a new camera; the getters read the pose back as it was built. Pitch measures tilt from straight down, from 0° to a maximum of 75°, so the view keeps ground in it. Bearing wraps into [0, 360).

The camera is also the projection and the tile selector. projectToScreen maps a coordinate to viewport pixels, screenToGroundCoordinate maps a pixel back to the ground, and groundMetersPerScreenPixel sizes a scale bar. The fitBounds constructor frames a bounding box inside an inset region you pass, so your own route cards and attribution never cover the destination.

Styles and overlays

A raster tile is a pre-rendered image. A vector tile carries geometry and style separately and is painted on the device. Vector base maps use named styles: Bright, Fiord, and Positron for OpenMapTiles-schema sources, and Carto Light and Carto Dark for the Sourdough source. Place names and road names are drawn from a glyph atlas; road shields are not drawn.

An overlay is geography plus a style, not a picture or a set of screen pixels. RoutePolyline, FilledPolygon, PointMarkers, PointPins, and TrafficFlow all carry coordinates, and the SDK projects them through the same camera as the tiles in every frame. Panning, zooming, rotating, and tilting keep the layers aligned because every frame re-projects the same geographic inputs.

Providers and credentials

Provider-backed capabilities reach you through a registry on MapSdk. Register an implementation, then call the contract methods: geocoding, routing, the distance matrix, place search, traffic incidents and flow, and raster tiles. The SDK includes MapQuest implementations for those contracts and URL-template providers for any raster or vector base map.

Provider keys are runtime inputs, not build inputs. Enter a key through your own settings surface, secure storage, or a launch value injected for one test session. There is no local.properties, Info.plist, or .xcconfig field for a key, and no release artifact carries one. A key you apply is held for the session and optionally remembered in the platform’s secure store, never in your project.

Map concepts

This page explains the ideas the SDK’s calls are built on: positions, the world square, tiles, zoom, the camera, styles, and overlays. The guides use these ideas without defining them. Read this page once, then continue with Your first map.

Positions and regions

A position is a GeographicCoordinate: latitude and longitude in decimal degrees on the WGS 84 ellipsoid. Latitude runs from -90 to 90; longitude runs from -180 to 180.

A region is a BoundingBox between a south-west and a north-east corner, each one a coordinate. A box never spans the antimeridian. If a region crosses it, encode the region as two adjacent boxes.

The examples use Kotlin field spelling. Each binding uses its platform’s spelling for the same records.

import uniffi.rustic_maps.BoundingBox
import uniffi.rustic_maps.GeographicCoordinate

val capitolPark = GeographicCoordinate(38.5766, -121.4944)
val downtownSacramento = BoundingBox(
    southWest = GeographicCoordinate(38.5700, -121.5030),
    northEast = GeographicCoordinate(38.5850, -121.4850),
)

The world square

The SDK does not draw in latitude and longitude. Before anything is placed on screen, a coordinate is projected onto the Web Mercator world: a square where every position becomes two numbers in [0, 1]. The horizontal number is zero on the antimeridian and grows eastward. The vertical number is zero at the north pole and grows southward.

Only part of the ellipsoid fits in that square. The projection stops at about 85.05° north and south, and latitudes beyond the cutoff clamp to the edge. The top and bottom of the world square are therefore not the poles, and a coordinate near a pole sits on the boundary rather than beyond it.

Mercator also changes scale across the map: it stretches the ground farther from the equator. At a given zoom, the ground distance covered by one screen pixel shrinks with the cosine of the center latitude. The camera answers that distance for a scale bar through groundMetersPerScreenPixel.

Tiles

A tile is one payload at one zoom level. Its address is a TileKey: a column, a row counted from the north, and the zoom level. This is the web-mercator XYZ scheme. At zoom 0 the whole world is one tile, and each level doubles the columns and rows, so zoom level z has 2^z columns and 2^z rows. A coordinate’s address is the tile cell that contains its position in the world square.

A raster tile is a pre-rendered image. The contract carries one as RasterTileData: the tile address, an image format (Png or Jpeg), a tile resolution, and the encoded bytes. Standard is the plain form; Retina is the @2x form with twice the texels per edge for the same logical tile span, which is what a high-density screen wants.

A vector tile carries geometry and style rather than pixels. Its vertices are stored in the tile’s own space, with x to the right and y down inside the tile. The SDK converts each vertex through the tile’s web-mercator address into a GeographicCoordinate, so vector geometry and your own overlays share one coordinate space. The renderer paints a vector base map with a named style. Bright, Fiord, and Positron style OpenMapTiles-schema sources; Carto Light and Carto Dark style the Sourdough source.

Either kind of tile is addressed, fetched, and reused by the same key. When the view moves, the SDK asks for the tiles the view now covers and keeps the ones it already holds.

Zoom is continuous

A camera’s zoom is a number, not a whole tile level, and each unit doubles the on-screen scale. The camera accepts zoom 0 through 24.

The tile grid changes only at whole levels, so a smooth pinch gesture passes through fractional zoom while the SDK picks the nearest whole level for a tile fetch: tileZoomLevel. To ask which tiles the view covers, use visibleTileKeys, which lists every tile at a chosen level whose area intersects the visible ground, sorted row-major from the north. A rotated or tilted view can cover tiles you would not guess from the center alone, so read the list instead of computing a rectangle.

The camera

A MapCamera is an anchored pose made of four values.

ValueWhat it means
centerThe ground point rendered at the viewport center
zoom_levelScale; continuous, and each unit doubles the on-screen scale
bearing_degreesThe compass direction the top of the viewport points to, clockwise from north, wrapped into [0, 360)
pitch_degreesTilt from straight down; zero is top-down, and the maximum is 75 degrees so the view keeps ground in it

The camera carries no setters. A new view is a new camera; the getters read the pose back as it was built.

import uniffi.rustic_maps.GeographicCoordinate
import uniffi.rustic_maps.MapCamera

val camera = MapCamera(
    center = GeographicCoordinate(38.5766, -121.4944),
    zoomLevel = 12.0,
    bearingDegrees = 0.0,
    pitchDegrees = 0.0,
)

A camera is also the projection and the tile selector, not only a description. projectToScreen maps a coordinate to viewport pixels, and screenToGroundCoordinate maps a pixel back to the ground, returning nothing when the pixel’s ray misses the ground. Both use the camera’s pose, so your own UI and the renderer place things on the same pixel without duplicating the math.

The second constructor, fitBounds, builds a camera that frames a bounding box: top-down and north-up, zoomed to the largest level that keeps the whole box inside the inset region you pass. Insets are the pixels your own UI keeps clear, such as a route card, a sheet panel, or an attribution label, so the box never hides beneath them.

Overlays are geography

Everything drawn on top of the tiles is an overlay: a MapOverlay record with a kind and the payload that kind reads.

KindPayload
RoutePolylinecoordinates, a polyline in traversal order
FilledPolygonringCoordinates, one outer ring in traversal order
PointMarkers and PointPinspointMarkerPositions, one coordinate per marker
TrafficFlowtrafficFlowSegments, traffic records whose shapeCoordinates are coordinates

The payload is the point: a list of GeographicCoordinate. An overlay is not a picture and not a set of screen pixels. It is geography plus a style (a color, a line width, a marker radius), and the SDK projects it through the same camera as the tiles in every frame.

That shared space is why an overlay needs no conversion work from your application. A calculated route carries its geometry as coordinates on its steps; flatten those shapes into one list and a RoutePolyline draws over the roads. A place returned by search carries a coordinate; put it in pointMarkerPositions and the marker sits on that place. Panning, zooming, rotating, and tilting keep the two layers aligned because every frame re-projects the same geographic inputs.

A frame in order

A frame is one pass through the same few steps:

  1. You choose a MapCamera pose.
  2. The camera lists the tiles the view covers and maps every overlay coordinate into the viewport.
  3. The SDK fetches the missing tiles, draws them, then draws the overlays through the same camera.
  4. A new pose repeats the pass; the coordinate space never changes.

Once those steps are clear, the guides are applications of them. Start with Your first map, then continue to Search and routing, Turn-by-turn navigation, and Offline maps.

How it works

The SDK is one Rust core behind one generated interface. This page describes that interface’s architecture: the data model, the camera and tile pipeline, the provider registry, the renderer, navigation, and offline routing. Every public type and call named here is part of the FFI contract.

Coordinates and the camera

A position is a GeographicCoordinate: latitude and longitude in decimal degrees on the WGS 84 ellipsoid. A region is a BoundingBox between a south-west and a north-east corner, and a box never spans the antimeridian.

The camera is a MapCamera value: an anchored pose of center, zoom, bearing, and pitch. The ground point under the center sits at the viewport center, zoom and pitch are clamped, and bearing wraps into the range from 0 up to but not including 360 degrees.

Camera attributeWhat it means
centerThe coordinate anchored at the viewport center
zoom_levelScale; a continuous level, not necessarily a whole number
bearing_degreesRotation clockwise from north
pitch_degreesTilt from top-down (0) toward the horizon

A camera carries no setters. A new pose is a new constructor call, and the attribute getters read the state back as it was built. The second constructor, fitBounds, frames a bounding box inside the inset region you give it: top-down, north-up, zoomed to the largest level that keeps the whole box visible, and anchored on the inset region’s center. Insets are the pixels your own UI keeps clear, so route cards and attribution never hide the destination.

The camera answers screen mappings without drawing. projectToScreen and screenToGroundCoordinate convert between a coordinate and viewport pixels, visibleTileKeys lists the tiles the view covers, and groundMetersPerScreenPixel sizes a scale bar.

Zoom levels and tiles

A tile is one payload at a fixed zoom, addressed by a TileKey: a column, a row counted from the north, and the zoom level. The addressing is the web-mercator XYZ scheme. At zoom 0 the world is one tile, and each level doubles the columns and rows.

The camera’s zoom is continuous, so it answers two different questions. tileZoomLevel gives the nearest whole level a tile fetch should use. visibleTileKeys gives every tile at a chosen level that intersects the visible ground, sorted row-major from the north.

A raster tile is a pre-rendered image. The contract carries it as RasterTileData with its encoded bytes, an image format (PNG or JPEG), and a resolution: Standard, or Retina for the doubled-texel @2x form.

A vector tile carries geometry and style separately from the pixels. The renderer decodes it, styles it with a named style, and draws it over the raster tiles and beneath the overlay list. Installing a vector base map on the map view with setVectorTileSource replaces any earlier vector base. The scheduler fetches and decodes each tile once and restyles it from cached geometry when the style changes or the camera crosses a style zoom stop, so it never refetches a tile for either. Bright, Fiord, and Positron style OpenMapTiles-schema sources; Carto Light and Carto Dark style the Sourdough source. Place names and road names are drawn from a glyph atlas; road shields are not drawn.

The architecture at a glance

your application
      │  Kotlin / Swift / TypeScript / JavaScript
      ▼
generated bindings  ── the UniFFI UDL contract (one surface, four platforms)
      │
      ▼
Rust core
  ├── provider registry   provider lookup and capability routing
  ├── provider adapters   vendor URLs, credentials, status mapping, attribution
  ├── camera + renderer   camera math, tile scheduling, GPU raster and vector paint
  ├── navigation          turn-by-turn reducer (pure, event-driven)
  ├── tile cache          disk response cache (SQLite, LRU byte budget)
  └── offline routing     archive reader + A* routing + tile pack manager

The browser build compiles the same core modules to WebAssembly and adds one layer the native targets do not need: a canvas binding that owns the WebGPU device and a fetch transport that replaces the native HTTP stack. Everything above that layer — camera math, tile scheduling, routing, navigation — is the same code the phone builds run.

Threading and lifecycle

The renderer draws only when asked. The native MapView owns a frame pump: it draws on camera, overlay, and tile changes, and skips a frame when isFrameSettled reports that nothing would change. The WebAssembly surface has no pump; your page calls renderFrame on each change. A still map therefore costs no frames.

  • Async calls (search, forwardGeocode, calculateRoute, tile fetches) suspend and resume on the platform’s own async runtime: Kotlin coroutines, Swift concurrency, or JavaScript promises. They are safe to call from the main thread.
  • Navigation callbacks are delivered in registration order on the runtime that produced the location update. Do no blocking work in them; hand results to your UI layer.
  • Drawing is single-flight: one draw may be in flight per surface, and a second call while it runs reports RenderingSurfaceUnavailable. A render pump should skip a frame when isFrameSettled reports nothing changed.
  • Surface lifecycle is attach, resize, draw, detach. Attaching without a usable platform surface throws; detach before the platform view goes away. Re-attach after you apply a credential, because a keyless start cannot draw provider imagery.

The provider registry

Provider-backed capability reaches you through MapSdk, an object with no providers at construction. You register implementations, then call the contract methods: forward and reverse geocoding, routing, the distance matrix, place search, traffic incidents, traffic flow, and raster tiles. Every call resolves through the registry. A call into a contract with no registration throws ProviderNotConfigured naming the contract.

Registration paths:

  • setProviderCredential installs the map-platform provider set from one API key, with the SDK defaults for rate limiting and retries.
  • setProviderCredentialWithTileCache installs the same set and wraps raster tiles in the disk response cache.
  • registerUrlTemplateRasterTileSource installs any web-mercator XYZ raster tileset from a {z}/{x}/{y} URL template, with no provider key.
  • registerGeocodingProviderFromForeign and registerRasterTileProviderFromForeign install an implementation your own Kotlin or Swift code supplies through the GeocodingProvider and RasterTileProvider interfaces.

Registration is per object. Re-registering the provider set replaces every slot; re-registering a URL-template raster source replaces the raster-tile slot, keeps every other slot serving, and drops any installed tile cache. A second MapSdk object needs its own registration.

The ten provider contracts include elevation. This binding surface exposes no elevation call, so no elevation provider is registered through these paths.

Supported providers

Capability comes from whichever provider you register. These ship today:

ProviderWhat it answersCredential
MapQuestgeocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, distance matrix, place search, traffic incidents, traffic flow, raster tilesAPI key
OpenStreetMap US (Sourdough)vector tilesnone
OpenFreeMapvector tilesnone
OpenStreetMap Standardraster tilesnone

The keyless vector and raster sources back the live demo’s base map; they carry their own attribution and usage terms, which the SDK surfaces alongside the imagery.

Adding a provider is a provider implementation plus a registration. Your application’s calls stay the same.

The cache path

setProviderCredentialWithTileCache installs the provider set and wraps the raster-tile contract in a disk response cache: a SQLite database at a path you own, under an absolute byte budget. A cache hit answers from disk, and a cache miss goes to the network and back-fills.

Cached tile responses are retained under the tiles category’s time-to-live, 30 calendar days by default. That default is also the imagery provider’s terms ceiling. setRasterTileCacheTimeToLive tunes the value, an override above the ceiling is accepted and clamped, and rasterTileCacheTerms reads back three values: the effective time-to-live, the provider’s declared ceiling, and the category default. The byte budget is fixed when the store opens, so changing it means registering again, and a fresh registration starts at the category default.

Raster imagery is the layer the cache holds. Offline routing is a separate layer with its own archive.

One contract, four platforms

One UniFFI UDL file defines the surface, and it is the single source of truth: the Kotlin, Swift, React Native, and WebAssembly bindings are all generated from it. The contract changes addition-only: an existing member keeps its signature and meaning, and a release adds members and records. The changelog records what each release adds.

PlatformHow you call the contract
Android (Kotlin)Suspend functions and typed records; failures are the contract’s SdkError variants
iOS (Swift)Async throwing methods and records
React NativePromise-returning TurboModule methods with lower camel case field names
WebAssemblyTypeScript classes and records over the wasm module, with the same names and field spellings as the native bindings

Plain data crosses as records and enums. The error model crosses as the SdkError variants the failing call can produce, with verbatim detail text. getSdkCompiledVersion on every surface answers the compiled SDK version, so a diagnostics screen can compare the loaded core with the artifacts your application shipped.

The error model

Every failure crosses the contract as one SdkError variant carrying a verbatim detail string. The retry column separates transient failures from input and configuration failures.

VariantMeaningRetry?
NetworkRequestFailedThe transport failedYes, with backoff
RateLimitExhaustedYour own token bucket is emptyYes, after the next refill
ProviderRequestRejectedThe provider refused the request (quota, bad input)No; fix the request or the plan
ResponseParsingFailureThe provider answered something unusableNo; report it verbatim
ProviderNotConfiguredNo implementation is registered for that capabilityNo; register one
InvalidCoordinateInputA coordinate, viewport, or box failed validationNo; fix the input
InvalidRenderInputAn overlay or surface input is unusableNo; fix the input
RenderingSurfaceUnavailableThe surface could not draw this frameYes, on the next frame
InvalidNavigationInputA route or navigation policy failed validationNo; fix the input
CacheOperationFailureA cache read, write, or eviction failedNo; the detail names the cause
OfflineRoutingFailureAn offline archive failed validation or could not be readNo; fix the archive

Surface the detail string as it arrives: it names the provider’s own reason and is the text support asks for. Never retry a non-retryable variant unchanged.

Navigation state

Routing returns a Route: legs between consecutive waypoints, and steps inside each leg, each carrying its distance, duration, maneuver label, and instruction texts. Navigation consumes that value rather than extending it.

Navigator holds a trip. You start one with startNavigation(route, unitSystem, stepAdvancePolicy, deviationPolicy) and deliver one position fix at a time with updateLocation. The controller publishes four topics: banner instructions, speech triggers, deviation status, and phase changes. A subscription is cancelled explicitly through its handle.

A trip has three phases: Navigating, OffRoute, and Arrived. Rerouting is not a phase; a trip moves between navigating and off route until it arrives. Deviation has two grades:

  • FullyOffRoute freezes progress until a graded fix recovers or a reroute replaces the route.
  • OffStepOnRoute means the fix is off the current step but still on a later part of the route, and the trip keeps navigating.

Guidance uses two policies you choose at trip start. StepAdvancePolicy decides when the trip moves to the next step, and DeviationPolicy decides when a fix counts as off route. A fix without a reported accuracy never advances a step and is never judged for deviation, so a simulated source must carry accuracy like a real one.

Instruction text has two channels. The banner channel carries the display text, and the speech channel carries the text-to-speech text through SpeechInstruction. The SDK decides when a line is newsworthy and supplies the text verbatim. Your application owns playback and synthesis, and utteranceId is a stable identity for deduplication.

A deviation asks for a replacement route through a reroute calculation gate. beginRerouteCalculation answers true when the request passes the in-flight, cooldown, and movement checks, applyReroute applies the replacement, and cancelRerouteCalculation abandons it. The trip state’s isCalculatingNewRoute reports the in-flight fact.

Offline routing

Offline routing answers from a compiled archive rather than a network round trip. The archive is built from an OpenStreetMap extract and is self-describing. It answers routes with an A* search over the archive’s graph and honors recorded turn restrictions. Maneuver text derives from the geometry where the extract carries no street names.

The direct route call is a contract function on every surface: offlineRouteFromArchiveBytes takes the archive bytes (a path is not needed, so the browser can call it) plus a start and an end coordinate. The offline routing decorator wraps your online provider when you choose to fall back; one compiled archive serves every target.

Where to go next

The guides apply these concepts in order: Your first map, Search and routing, Turn-by-turn navigation, and Offline maps.

Use the SDK from Rust

The map SDK is a Rust workspace. The same crates that back the Android, iOS, React Native and WebAssembly bindings can be used directly by a Rust application: the renderer, the camera and projection math, the provider traits, the navigation controller and the offline routing graph all live in Rust and have no platform dependency.

Crates

CrateWhat it provides
map-renderingThe camera and projection model, the raster tile scheduler, overlays, labels and the headless wgpu renderer
map-coreThe provider registry, provider contracts, offline routing and the shared SDK operations
geospatial-typesCoordinates, tiles, records and the shared error type
geospatial-traitsThe vendor-neutral provider traits a tileset, routing or geocoding service implements
map-navigationRoute walking, instruction generation, deviation and reroute policy
map-positioningPosition validation, course smoothing and the simulated position source
map-vector-tiles / map-glyphsMapbox Vector Tile decoding and glyph-atlas packing
map-offline-graph-archiveReading compiled offline routing graphs

The crates are consumed from the SDK source today; a registry package follows the first Rust release.

Camera and projection without a GPU

Camera math and projection are pure Rust and run anywhere:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use geospatial_types::GeographicCoordinate;
use map_rendering::{DEFAULT_FIELD_OF_VIEW_DEGREES, MapCamera, ViewportPixels};

let center = GeographicCoordinate::from_degrees(38.5766, -121.4944)?;
let camera = MapCamera::new(center, 12.0, 0.0, 0.0);
let viewport = ViewportPixels::new(1280.0, 720.0)
    .map_err(|detail| format!("invalid viewport: {detail}"))?;

let screen_point = camera.project_to_screen(
    &center,
    &viewport,
    DEFAULT_FIELD_OF_VIEW_DEGREES,
);
}

Rendering a frame

map-rendering’s headless renderer draws into an offscreen wgpu target: create a HeadlessTileRenderer over a GraphicsContext, resolve the camera’s visible tiles through a TileScheduler, and read the frame back as RGBA bytes. The renderer is the same one the native surfaces use, so what you see offscreen matches what a platform view presents.

The browser uses the same camera, overlay, label and vector-style modules; it binds them through a WebAssembly canvas adapter rather than a Rust surface.

Providers

Implement the vendor-neutral traits from geospatial-traits — a raster or vector tileset, a routing engine, a geocoding service, a distance matrix or traffic — and register them in the map-core registry. The registry is what the SDK’s operations dispatch through, so a Rust application and a platform binding share the same provider story. See Add a provider for the descriptor fields and the registration path.

Positioning

map-positioning::PositionController validates the fixes your OS source reports, smooths their course and tracks staleness, so a Rust application can feed the same stream to the renderer’s location layer, a follow camera and the navigation controller. SimulatedPositionSource walks a route for tests and demos:

cargo run -p map-positioning --example simulated_walk

Your first map

Install the SDK, register a map provider, and draw your first map. Choose your platform and follow the steps in order. The SDK calls in these steps compile against the FFI contract. If you are new to map SDKs, read Map concepts first: it explains tiles, zoom levels, the world coordinate system, and the camera these steps build on.

Before you start

  • Android Studio with the SDK 36 toolchain.
  • A project with minSdk = 24.
  • The release AARs copied into app/libs/.
  • A provider API key for the provider you register.

Install the artifact

In your application module’s build.gradle.kts, add the local AAR and the two runtime dependencies the Kotlin bindings need:

repositories {
    flatDir { dirs("libs") }
}

dependencies {
    implementation(files("libs/rustic-maps-sdk-android-v0.1.0.aar"))
    // The MapView wrapper is a second AAR and depends on the bindings above.
    implementation(files("libs/rustic-maps-sdk-android-ui-v0.1.0.aar"))
    implementation("net.java.dev.jna:jna:5.18.1@aar")   // the UniFFI runtime
    implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core:1.10.2")
}

Keep the version in each file name exact.

Build the SDK and register the provider

Construct the SDK object and install the map-platform provider set in one call:

import uniffi.rustic_maps.MapSdk

val mapSdk = MapSdk()
// The key belongs to the provider you registered; see "Choosing a provider".
mapSdk.setProviderCredential(providerApiKey)

The call throws the provider’s message when the key is refused. Surface it in your error state instead of continuing.

Read the key at runtime: from your own secure configuration or a settings screen, never from source and never baked into the build. The SDK has no build field for a credential.

Show the map in your layout

The package ships a lifecycle-aware MapView that owns the surface, the frame pump, resizing, gestures and the camera animation. Drop it into your composition and give it the SDK:

import com.angoratek.rusticmaps.compose.MapView

MapView(
    sdk = mapSdk,
    listener = mapViewListener,
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(),
)

Place it with AndroidView when you are not using Compose; the widget is a plain SurfaceView subclass. Either way you never touch a native window pointer, never attach, and never pump frames — the view does all of it, and pauses itself when the host stops or the window detaches.

Open the map

Set the camera the view draws with. The shared demo camera on every platform is Capitol Park, Sacramento at zoom 12, north-up and top-down:

val mapCamera = MapCameraPose(
    latitudeDegrees = 38.5766,
    longitudeDegrees = -121.4944,
    zoomLevel = 12.0,
    bearingDegrees = 0.0,
    pitchDegrees = 0.0,
)
mapView.setCamera(mapCamera)

animateCamera eases to a pose over a duration. fitBounds frames a box inside a viewport with edge insets. Use them to keep search results and the route preview in view.

Pan the camera from a gesture

Gesture recognition stays in your platform view; the camera algebra is the SDK’s. Forward the drag delta to the camera member and keep the pose it returns (the ground point the pointer grabbed becomes the new center):

val pannedCamera = camera.panByScreenPixels(
    deltaXPixels = dragDeltaXPixels,
    deltaYPixels = dragDeltaYPixels,
    viewport = ViewportSize(
        widthPixels = viewportWidthPixels,
        heightPixels = viewportHeightPixels,
    ),
    fieldOfViewDegrees = 60.0,
)
center = pannedCamera.center()

MapView applies pan, pinch, and rotation from its own gesture handlers. Call this member when you drive the camera from your own control or from a test.

zoomByLevelsAroundScreenPoint and rotateByDegreesAroundScreenPoint apply the pinch and twist deltas with the same focal-point correction, so every platform computes identical results.

Add your first overlay

Draw more than tiles by setting the overlay list the surface draws every frame. A route polyline over the demo’s two waypoints (Capitol Park to Tower Bridge):

import uniffi.rustic_maps.GeographicCoordinate
import uniffi.rustic_maps.MapOverlay
import uniffi.rustic_maps.MapOverlayKind
import uniffi.rustic_maps.OverlayColor

mapView.setOverlays(
    listOf(
        MapOverlay(
            kind = MapOverlayKind.ROUTE_POLYLINE,
            coordinates = listOf(
                GeographicCoordinate(38.5766, -121.4944),
                GeographicCoordinate(38.5802, -121.5083),
            ),
            rgbaColor = OverlayColor(red = 0.2, green = 0.4, blue = 0.9, alpha = 0.9),
            widthPixels = 3.0,
            // The other payload fields stay null for this kind.
            ringCoordinates = null,
            pointMarkerPositions = null,
            pointMarkerRadiusPixels = null,
            trafficFlowSegments = null,
        ),
    ),
)

setOverlays is the bulk call for a list you own whole: it replaces the drawn list in one go. For overlays you keep across frames, address them individually: addOverlay returns an opaque identifier, updateOverlay replaces that entry in its draw position, and removeOverlay returns whether it was present:

val routeOverlayId = mapView.addOverlay(routePolylineOverlay)
// ...later, when the route changes:
mapView.updateOverlay(routeOverlayId, replacementPolylineOverlay)
// ...and when it is dismissed:
mapView.removeOverlay(routeOverlayId)

Identifiers are monotonic per view and never reused; clearOverlays() clears both the bulk list and the addressed overlays.

Before you start

  • Xcode with Swift 5.10 (swift-tools-version: 5.10).
  • A project with an iOS 17 deployment target.
  • The iOS release artifact.
  • A provider API key for the provider you register.

Add the release’s Swift package and both of its products: RusticMapsSDK (the generated bindings) and MapNativeCoreUI (the map view). The package manifest pins the checksummed XCFramework as its binary target:

// Package.swift
// swift-tools-version: 5.10
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "MyMapApp",
    dependencies: [
        // The package the release publishes: a generated branch manifest whose
        // binaryTarget pins the XCFramework URL and checksum.
        .package(
            url: "https://github.com/angoratek/rustic-maps-sdk.git",
            branch: "swift-package"
        ),
    ],
    targets: [
        .executableTarget(
            name: "MyMapApp",
            // Both products ship in the same package: the bindings and the
            // map view.
            dependencies: [
                .product(name: "RusticMapsSDK", package: "rustic-maps-sdk"),
                .product(name: "MapNativeCoreUI", package: "rustic-maps-sdk"),
            ]
        )
    ]
)

Build the SDK and register the provider

Construct the SDK and register the provider:

import RusticMapsSDK

let mapSdk = MapSdk()
// The key belongs to the provider you registered; see "Choosing a provider".
try mapSdk.setProviderCredential(credential: providerApiKey)

The call throws the provider’s message when the key is refused.

Read the key at runtime: from app settings, a secure configuration store, or a launch environment for automated tests. Do not add it to Info.plist or to an .xcconfig that ships in the app.

Show the map in your layout

The MapNativeCoreUI package ships a MapView that owns the Metal surface, the frame pump, resizing, gestures and the camera animation. Put it in your view hierarchy and give it the SDK:

// `mapView` is the `MapNativeCoreUI.MapView` the package ships: it owns the
// Metal surface, the frame pump, resizing and gestures. Hand it the SDK and
// put it in your hierarchy.
mapView.sdk = mapSdk

SwiftUIMapView wraps the same view for SwiftUI hosts. You never create a surface handle, never attach, and never drive a display link — the view does all of it and tears itself down when it leaves the hierarchy.

Open the map

Set the camera the view draws with. The shared demo camera on every platform is Capitol Park, Sacramento at zoom 12, north-up and top-down:

let mapCamera = MapCameraPose(
    latitudeDegrees: 38.5766,
    longitudeDegrees: -121.4944,
    zoomLevel: 12.0,
    bearingDegrees: 0.0,
    pitchDegrees: 0.0
)
mapView.setCamera(mapCamera)

animateCamera eases to a pose over a duration. fitBounds frames a box inside a viewport with edge insets. Use them to keep search results and the route preview in view.

Pan the camera from a gesture

Keep the gesture recognizers in your view and forward their deltas to the camera member (the ground point the finger grabbed becomes the new center):

let pannedCamera = try camera.panByScreenPixels(
    deltaXPixels: dragDeltaPixels.width,
    deltaYPixels: dragDeltaPixels.height,
    viewport: viewport,
    fieldOfViewDegrees: fieldOfViewDegrees
)
let pannedCenter = pannedCamera.center()

zoomByLevelsAroundScreenPoint and rotateByDegreesAroundScreenPoint apply pinch and twist deltas with the same focal-point correction.

Fit the map to what you show

For a bounded region, let the camera fit the box instead of hand-tuning zoom:

let fittedCamera = try MapCamera.fitBounds(
    boundingBox: regionBox,
    viewport: viewport,
    edgeInsets: EdgeInsets(
        left: 224, top: 48, right: 48, bottom: 96
    ),
    maximumZoomLevel: 22
)

Before you start

  • An initialized React Native (bare workflow) application on Android arm64-v8a or iOS.
  • The release tarball.
  • A provider API key for the provider you register.

Install the artifact

Install the release tarball you downloaded; no registry is involved:

npm install ./rustic-maps-sdk-rn-v0.1.0.tgz

The package carries the TurboModule glue. Link it with your React Native version’s normal autolinking, and run pod install on iOS.

Build the SDK and register the provider

The package owns one native SDK per process. Create it with MapsSdk.create() and register the provider’s credential:

import { MapsSdk } from '@angoratek/rustic-maps-sdk/MapsSdk';

export async function createMapSdk(providerKey, providerApiKey) {
  const mapSdk = await MapsSdk.create();
  const registration = await mapSdk.setProviderCredential(
    providerKey,
    providerApiKey,
  );
  if (!registration.isApplied) {
    throw new Error(registration.detailText);
  }
  return mapSdk;
}

A refused credential resolves with isApplied: false and the provider’s verbatim detailText, so surface it in your error state rather than continuing.

Choosing a provider

The credential call is the same on every platform; what changes is which provider you register and where its key comes from.

ProviderWhat it servesCredential
MapQuestgeocoding, search, routing, the distance matrix, traffic, and raster tilesan API key from the MapQuest developer console
A URL-template raster source (OpenStreetMap, a self-hosted tile server)base-map tiles onlyusually none — some ask for a User-Agent instead
A URL-template vector source (OpenFreeMap, OpenStreetMap US)a styled vector base with labelsnone
Your own providerwhichever contracts you implementwhatever your implementation needs

Register the one you intend to use, then apply its credential:

import { MapsSdk } from '@angoratek/rustic-maps-sdk/MapsSdk';

// MapQuest, with a key the user entered in your settings screen. A keyless
// URL-template base map needs no credential at all: register that source and
// its tiles flow.
const mapSdk = await MapsSdk.create();
await mapSdk.setProviderCredential('mapquest', providerApiKey);

A keyless base map still draws, and search, routing, and traffic respond only once a provider that serves those contracts has a credential. Nothing here ties your app to MapQuest: the providers your app registers decide what is available, and the calls above stay the same.

Take the key at runtime: a settings screen, secure storage, or a launch environment for automated tests. Do not bake it into the JS bundle or a native build file.

Draw a map surface

The package ships a typed <MapView> component over the native widget (Android SurfaceView, iOS CAMetalLayer). It owns the surface lifecycle, frame pump, gestures, camera calls, id-addressed overlays, and the callback set, so the host application only composes it. The package also owns the one native SDK instance; create it with MapsSdk.create() before you mount the view, which attaches to it as soon as it is available.

import { useRef } from 'react';
import { MapView, type MapViewHandle } from '@angoratek/rustic-maps-sdk/MapView';

// Hold the handle to drive the camera, overlays and location layer.
const mapViewRef = useRef<MapViewHandle | null>(null);

<MapView
  ref={mapViewRef}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  topBarInsetPixels={topBarInsetPixels}
  bottomBarInsetPixels={bottomBarInsetPixels}
  onMapReady={() => { /* the first frame presented */ }}
  onCameraChanged={(camera, isGestureDriven) => { /* reflect the pose */ }}
  onError={(failure) => { /* failure.phase, failure.message */ }}
/>;

Use the component as the documented path: it keeps one SDK instance and one frame pump. The generated contract classes from the package root remain available for advanced use such as a custom host view.

Check the installation with the compiled-version probe:

import { getSdkCompiledVersion } from '@angoratek/rustic-maps-sdk';

getSdkCompiledVersion();
// → "0.1.0": the Rust core loaded and answered through the TurboModule.

Open the map

The component’s handle takes the same camera values the other tabs use. The shared demo camera on every platform is Capitol Park, Sacramento at zoom 12, north-up and top-down:

const mapCamera = {
  latitudeDegrees: 38.5766,
  longitudeDegrees: -121.4944,
  zoomLevel: 12.0,
  bearingDegrees: 0.0,
  pitchDegrees: 0.0,
};
mapView.setCamera(mapCamera);

animateCamera and fitBounds are on the same handle, with the same signatures the other tabs show.

Pan the camera from a gesture

The generated MapCamera carries the same gesture members on the JavaScript side. The package’s native views call them for their own gestures; reach for them when you drive the camera from a control of your own or from a test:

const pannedCamera = camera.panByScreenPixels(
  dragDeltaXPixels,
  dragDeltaYPixels,
  viewport,
  fieldOfViewDegrees,
);
const pannedCenter = pannedCamera.center();

zoomByLevelsAroundScreenPoint and rotateByDegreesAroundScreenPoint apply pinch and twist deltas with the same focal-point correction.

Where to continue

The camera block is the first step of the worked example that runs through these guides. The same mapCamera, mapSdk, and mapView continue through Search and routing, Turn-by-turn navigation, and Offline maps with the same names. Continue there once this map draws.

Before you start

  • A Chromium-based browser with WebGPU: flag-free in Chromium since 113, Safari from 26, and Firefox from 141 on desktop.
  • The release package for WebAssembly.

A page needs a provider key only for live search, routing, and imagery. Keyless, it renders recorded tiles and recorded places.

Install the artifact

Unpack the release and serve its directory from any static file server over HTTPS or localhost:

npm install ./rustic-maps-sdk-web-v0.1.0.tgz
cp -r node_modules/@angoratek/rustic-maps-sdk-web ./web
python3 -m http.server 8000   # any static server; localhost is fine

Start the SDK and show the map on a canvas

One page creates one SDK root. Provider registration is a separate free call whose first argument is the provider key from the shared registry; read the credential at runtime — a settings form, a server-issued token, or a test’s environment — never from the bundle.

The browser has no native view to drop into a layout. You supply a <canvas> element and hand it, plus the SDK root, to MapView. The view claims the element, acquires the WebGPU device, and renders tiles fetched from a same-origin path you host. The page keeps pointer handling; the view owns the surface and the frame.

<canvas id="map-canvas"></canvas>

import init, { MapsSdk, MapView, registerProvider } from './web/map_web_bindings.js';

await init();
const mapSdk = await MapsSdk.create();
registerProvider('mapquest', providerCredential);

const canvas = /** @type {HTMLCanvasElement} */ (
  document.querySelector('#map-canvas')
);
const mapView = new MapView(canvas, mapSdk);
const adapterDescription = await mapView.initialize();
console.log(`Maps SDK ready (version ${mapSdk.compiledVersion}) on ${adapterDescription}`);

The demo skips the registerProvider call until a visitor supplies a key; recorded tiles and recorded places fill the map meanwhile.

The status probe returns the same version string the native surfaces do. The view’s tile resolution follows the device pixel ratio; the optional third constructor argument pins it (new MapView(canvas, mapSdk, TileResolution.Retina)). The canvas fetches raster tiles from the same-origin /tiles/{zoom}_{tileX}_{tileY}.png path, so serve your imagery there.

If initialize() fails in a browser without WebGPU, give the page the documented degradation message (name navigator.gpu and the missing capability; link the MDN compatibility table) — never a user-agent sniff.

Open the map

Set the camera the view draws with, then present a frame. The shared demo camera on every platform is Capitol Park, Sacramento at zoom 12, north-up and top-down:

const mapCamera = new MapCamera(38.5766, -121.4944, 12.0, 0.0, 0.0);
const fieldOfViewDegrees = 60.0;
const frameStatistics = await mapView.renderFrame(mapCamera, fieldOfViewDegrees);

renderFrame takes the camera by value, so build a fresh MapCamera for each changed pose. The other tabs hand their view a camera and let it pump frames; the browser page calls renderFrame itself on every change.

Project and unproject

The same camera projects and unprojects without rendering:

const screenPoint = camera.projectToScreen(
  latitudeDegrees,
  longitudeDegrees,
  canvas.width,
  canvas.height,
  fieldOfViewDegrees,
);
const groundCoordinate = camera.screenToGroundCoordinate(
  screenPoint.x,
  screenPoint.y,
  canvas.width,
  canvas.height,
  fieldOfViewDegrees,
);
const tileKeys = camera.visibleTileKeys(
  canvas.width,
  canvas.height,
  fieldOfViewDegrees,
  tileZoom,
);

These methods return plain objects with lower-camel-case fields; the generated declarations describe each shape.

Pan the camera from a gesture

There is no gesture layer on this surface: keep pointer capture, wheel and touch handling in your page and forward the travel to the camera member. It returns the resulting pose as a plain object (the ground point the pointer grabbed becomes the new center):

const pannedCamera = camera.panByScreenPixels(
  deltaXPixels,
  deltaYPixels,
  canvas.width,
  canvas.height,
  fieldOfViewDegrees,
);
const pannedCenter = pannedCamera.center();

zoomByLevelsAroundScreenPoint and rotateByDegreesAroundScreenPoint apply pinch and twist deltas with the same focal-point correction. Equivalent free functions (panCameraByScreenPixels, zoomCameraByLevelsAroundScreenPoint, rotateCameraByDegreesAroundScreenPoint) are also available.

Add your first overlay

Draw more than tiles by setting the overlay list the view draws every frame. The descriptor uses the browser’s field spelling: color, not the native tabs’ rgbaColor.

const routeOverlay = {
  kind: 'routePolyline',
  coordinates: [
    { latitude: 38.5766, longitude: -121.4944 },
    { latitude: 38.5802, longitude: -121.5083 },
  ],
  color: { red: 0.2, green: 0.4, blue: 0.9, alpha: 0.9 },
  widthPixels: 3.0,
};
mapView.setOverlays([routeOverlay]);

setOverlays replaces the drawn list in one go. For an overlay you keep across frames, addOverlay returns an opaque identifier, updateOverlay replaces that entry in its draw position, and removeOverlay returns whether it was present.

Where to continue

The camera block is the first step of the worked example that runs through these guides. The same mapCamera, mapSdk, and mapView continue through Search and routing, Turn-by-turn navigation, and Offline maps with the same names. Continue there once this map draws.

What you verified

You built the SDK entry object, registered a map provider with your own key, and drew map imagery through the SDK renderer. The FFI contract carries every member you called, and the generated API reference documents them.

Search and routing

Turn a typed query into places, plan a route between them, and draw it on the map. This guide continues from Your first map; every code block compiles against the FFI contract.

Resolve a query into places

Provider calls on Android are Kotlin suspend funs. Run them from a coroutine scope. Each plan field resolves the text the user typed:

val originPlace: Place = mapSdk.forwardGeocode(originSearchQuery).firstOrNull()
    ?: return null
val destinationPlace: Place = mapSdk.forwardGeocode(destinationSearchQuery).firstOrNull()
    ?: return null

forwardGeocode returns every candidate the provider resolved, most likely first. suggest returns fast completion candidates while the user types, and search returns full results for a settled query. Both search calls take an optional BoundingBox that restricts the search.

Plan the route

calculateRoute takes the ordered waypoints and the routing options. The request is the same on every platform: two waypoints, a pedestrian route, the fastest strategy, metric units, and no avoids.

val routeOptions = RouteOptions(
    transportationMode = TransportationMode.PEDESTRIAN,
    routeStrategy = RouteStrategy.FASTEST,
    unitSystem = UnitSystem.METRIC,
    avoidOptions = AvoidOptions(
        tollRoads = false,
        limitedAccessHighways = false,
        ferries = false,
        unpavedRoads = false,
    ),
    departureTimestampSeconds = null,
)
val plannedRoute = mapSdk.calculateRoute(
    waypoints = listOf(originPlace.coordinate, destinationPlace.coordinate),
    routeOptions = routeOptions,
)

The returned Route carries the total distance and duration, the bounding box, and one leg per waypoint pair with its maneuver steps.

Frame the route preview

Let the camera fit the route’s bounding box through the fitBounds constructor instead of hand-tuning zoom:

import uniffi.rustic_maps.EdgeInsets
import uniffi.rustic_maps.MapCamera
import uniffi.rustic_maps.ViewportSize

val fittedCamera = try {
    MapCamera.fitBounds(
        route.boundingBox,
        ViewportSize(widthPixels, heightPixels),
        EdgeInsets(left = 224.0, top = 48.0, right = 48.0, bottom = 96.0),
        maximumZoomLevel = 22.0,
    )
} catch (sdkException: SdkException) {
    // A refused fit (no positive box area, unusable insets) surfaces
    // verbatim; keep the previous camera.
    null
}

The insets you pass are the pixels your overlays keep clear, so the destination never hides under your own panels.

Draw the route

Build one route-polyline overlay from the planned geometry and hand it to the map view. The overlay step in Your first map covers the descriptor’s other fields.

val routeOverlay = MapOverlay(
    kind = MapOverlayKind.ROUTE_POLYLINE,
    coordinates = plannedRoute.legs
        .flatMap { leg -> leg.steps }
        .flatMap { step -> step.shape },
    rgbaColor = null,
    widthPixels = null,
    ringCoordinates = null,
    pointMarkerPositions = null,
    pointMarkerRadiusPixels = null,
    trafficFlowSegments = null,
)
mapView.setOverlays(listOf(routeOverlay))

Then start a trip in Turn-by-turn navigation.

Group the calls with engines

The contract also groups these capabilities into small engine objects built over the same SDK. Each one delegates to the SDK, with the same typed failures and detail text as the MapSdk member it wraps:

import uniffi.rustic_maps.RoutingEngine
import uniffi.rustic_maps.SearchEngine

val searchEngine = SearchEngine(mapSdk)
val settledPlaces = searchEngine.search("Capitol Park", searchBoundary = null)

val routingEngine = RoutingEngine(mapSdk)
val plannedRoute = routingEngine.calculateRoute(waypoints, routeOptions)

Resolve a query into places

Provider calls on iOS throw on failure and await the provider:

let originResults = try await mapSdk.forwardGeocode(addressText: originSearchQuery)
let destinationResults = try await mapSdk.forwardGeocode(
    addressText: destinationSearchQuery
)
guard
    let originPlace = originResults.first,
    let destinationPlace = destinationResults.first
else {
    throw WalkthroughScenarioError.planFieldResolvedNoPlace
}

suggest returns fast completion candidates for a query under construction. search returns full results for a settled query. Both take an optional BoundingBox.

Plan the route

let routeOptions = RouteOptions(
    transportationMode: .pedestrian,
    routeStrategy: .fastest,
    unitSystem: .metric,
    avoidOptions: AvoidOptions(
        tollRoads: false,
        limitedAccessHighways: false,
        ferries: false,
        unpavedRoads: false
    ),
    departureTimestampSeconds: nil
)
let plannedRoute = try await mapSdk.calculateRoute(
    waypoints: [originPlace.coordinate, destinationPlace.coordinate],
    routeOptions: routeOptions
)

The returned Route carries distance, duration, the bounding box, and one leg per waypoint pair with its steps.

Frame and draw the preview

Fit the camera to the route’s bounding box, as Your first map shows, then hand the route geometry to the map view’s overlay list:

let fittedCamera = try MapCamera.fitBounds(
    boundingBox: plannedRoute.boundingBox,
    viewport: viewport,
    edgeInsets: EdgeInsets(left: 224, top: 48, right: 48, bottom: 96),
    maximumZoomLevel: 22
)
pinnedFitBoundsCamera = fittedCamera

let routeOverlay = MapOverlay(
    kind: .routePolyline,
    coordinates: plannedRoute.legs
        .flatMap { leg in leg.steps }
        .flatMap { step in step.shape },
    rgbaColor: nil,
    widthPixels: nil,
    ringCoordinates: nil,
    pointMarkerPositions: nil,
    pointMarkerRadiusPixels: nil,
    trafficFlowSegments: nil
)
_ = mapView.setOverlays([routeOverlay])

Group the calls with engines

Each engine wraps the same SDK and keeps the typed failures and detail text:

let searchEngine = SearchEngine(mapSdk: mapSdk)
let settledPlaces = try await searchEngine.search(
    queryText: "Capitol Park",
    searchBoundary: nil
)

let routingEngine = RoutingEngine(mapSdk: mapSdk)
let plannedRoute = try await routingEngine.calculateRoute(
    waypoints: waypoints,
    routeOptions: routeOptions
)

Resolve a query into places

The package’s MapsSdk handle returns the contract’s search and routing calls as promises. Every record it resolves carries the same fields the other platforms see, in lower camel case:

const originPlace = (await mapSdk.forwardGeocode(originSearchQuery))[0] ?? null;
const destinationPlace =
  (await mapSdk.forwardGeocode(destinationSearchQuery))[0] ?? null;

A query that resolves to no place leaves the field null. The example stops before planning rather than inventing a coordinate.

Pass undefined or omit the boundary to search worldwide. Pass a BoundingBox with southWest and northEast corners to restrict the search. suggest returns completion candidates while the user types; search returns full results for a settled query.

Plan the route

const routeOptions: RouteOptions = {
  transportationMode: TransportationMode.Pedestrian,
  routeStrategy: RouteStrategy.Fastest,
  unitSystem: UnitSystem.Metric,
  avoidOptions: {
    tollRoads: false,
    limitedAccessHighways: false,
    ferries: false,
    unpavedRoads: false,
  },
  departureTimestampSeconds: undefined,
};
const plannedRoute = await mapSdk.calculateRoute(
  [originPlace.coordinate, destinationPlace.coordinate],
  routeOptions,
);

The route carries distanceMeters, durationSeconds, the bounding box and one leg per waypoint pair with its steps.

A rejected promise carries the typed SdkError. Surface it in your error state rather than retrying blindly; the rate limiter refills on its own.

Frame the route preview

The map view’s fitBounds takes the same inset story as the other tabs: 224 px clear on the left for the route card, 48 px top and right, 96 px bottom, clamped at zoom 22:

mapView.fitBounds(
  plannedRoute.boundingBox,
  { left: 224, top: 48, right: 48, bottom: 96 },
  22,
);

Draw the route

Build one route-polyline overlay from the planned geometry and hand it to the map view:

const routeOverlay: MapOverlay = {
  kind: MapOverlayKind.RoutePolyline,
  coordinates: plannedRoute.legs.flatMap(leg =>
    leg.steps.flatMap(step => step.shape),
  ),
};
await mapView.setOverlays([routeOverlay]);

Keep one SDK handle

The package handle exposes search, suggest, forwardGeocode, and calculateRoute directly, so a React Native screen needs no extra wrapper. The generated engine classes wrap a lower-level MapSdk instance, which would be a second SDK — with its own provider registry and tile cache — in the same process. Keep the single handle from the first map guide.

Register the provider at runtime

A browser page has no settings sheet. Provider registration is a free call; its first argument is the provider key from the shared registry. Take the credential from your own runtime source: a form, a server-issued token, or a test environment. Keyless, the demo searches recorded places and plans recorded routes.

import { registerProvider } from './web/map_web_bindings.js';

registerProvider('mapquest', providerCredential);

The calls below reject with the provider’s own error text when no provider is registered or the provider refuses.

Resolve the queries into places, then plan the route

forwardGeocode returns every candidate the provider resolved, most likely first. Its rows carry structuredAddressText, latitudeDegrees, and longitudeDegrees. suggestPlaces returns completion candidates, and searchPlaces returns full results for a settled query. The calculateRoute call takes two coordinates and uses the default request: automobile, fastest, metric.

import { forwardGeocode, calculateRoute } from './web/map_web_bindings.js';

const originSearchQuery = 'Capitol Park';
const destinationSearchQuery = 'Tower Bridge';

const originPlace = (await forwardGeocode(originSearchQuery))[0] ?? null;
const destinationPlace = (await forwardGeocode(destinationSearchQuery))[0] ?? null;
if (originPlace === null || destinationPlace === null) {
  throw new Error('the provider resolved no place for one of the queries');
}

const plannedRoute = await calculateRoute(
  originPlace.latitudeDegrees,
  originPlace.longitudeDegrees,
  destinationPlace.latitudeDegrees,
  destinationPlace.longitudeDegrees,
);

For a pedestrian route or explicit avoids, calculateRouteWithOptions takes the contract’s RouteOptions. The returned record has the same distanceMeters, durationSeconds, boundingBox, and legs-of-steps shape the other tabs read.

Frame the route preview

Let the camera fit the route’s bounding box through the same fitted constructor the native tabs use. The arguments are the box’s corners, the viewport, the edge insets in top/right/bottom/left order, and the zoom ceiling:

/** @type {any} */
const plannedRoute = route;
const viewportWidthPixels = window.innerWidth;
const viewportHeightPixels = window.innerHeight;
const topInsetPixels = 48.0;
const rightInsetPixels = 48.0;
const bottomInsetPixels = 96.0;
const leftInsetPixels = 224.0;
const maximumZoomLevel = 22.0;

const fittedCamera = MapCamera.fittingBounds(
  plannedRoute.boundingBox.southWest.latitude,
  plannedRoute.boundingBox.southWest.longitude,
  plannedRoute.boundingBox.northEast.latitude,
  plannedRoute.boundingBox.northEast.longitude,
  viewportWidthPixels,
  viewportHeightPixels,
  topInsetPixels,
  rightInsetPixels,
  bottomInsetPixels,
  leftInsetPixels,
  maximumZoomLevel,
);

The insets are the pixels your own panels keep clear, so the destination never hides under them. A refused fit throws the reason; keep the previous camera.

Draw the route

Build one route-polyline overlay from the planned geometry and hand it to the view. The browser descriptor spells the color field color, not the native tabs’ rgbaColor:

const plannedRoute = route;
const routeOverlay = {
  kind: 'routePolyline',
  coordinates: plannedRoute.legs.flatMap(
    (leg) => leg.steps.flatMap((step) => step.shape),
  ),
  color: { red: 0.16, green: 0.47, blue: 1.0, alpha: 0.95 },
  widthPixels: 6.0,
};
mapView.setOverlays([routeOverlay]);

Then start a trip in Turn-by-turn navigation.

Turn-by-turn navigation

Start a trip on a route, deliver position fixes, and receive turn-by-turn guidance: the banner instruction, speech triggers, deviation status, and phase. This guide turns the route you planned in Search and routing into a simulated Capitol Park to Tower Bridge drive. Every code block compiles against the FFI contract.

Build the controller and subscribe first

Subscribe before you start the trip, so you receive the initial instruction dispatch. The listener implements the four callbacks the contract carries:

import uniffi.rustic_maps.Navigator
import uniffi.rustic_maps.NavigationListener

class GuidanceListener(
    private val onInstruction: (NavigationInstruction) -> Unit,
