Each artifact file and SHA256SUMS.txt also have a .sigstore.json signature bundle, attached by the release workflow when it publishes a release; the checksum files above are always present.

What accompanies every release

Every version carries a per-file .sha256 sidecar, an aggregated SHA256SUMS.txt manifest covering all files, and a Sigstore signature bundle (.sigstore.json) per file and for SHA256SUMS.txt itself. A published version is immutable: a problem is fixed by a new version, never by replacing a file.

Verifying an artifact

Verify the checksum first, then the signature. The signature bundles bind the file to the release workflow and the vX.Y.Z tag, so the verification command pins both:

sha256sum --check SHA256SUMS.txt --ignore-missing

cosign verify-blob <artifact-file> \
  --bundle <artifact-file>.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity-regexp "<the identity printed by your download page>" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

The version page prints the exact identity string for its own tag. The --ignore-missing flag keeps the sha256sum run to the files you actually downloaded.

Installing from a release

The tutorials carry the per-platform install steps against these exact artifact names: the AAR for Android, the checksummed zip for the Swift Package Manager binary target, and the module archive for the wasm package. The npm packages ship the same generated trees with a manifest, licenses and notices.

To build the same packages from a checkout, each one has a script that produces the artifact the tutorials install —

PackageScriptOutput
Androidscripts/build-android.shthe bindings AAR and the MapView wrapper AAR
iOSscripts/build-ios.shthe XCFramework and the verified Swift package
React Nativescripts/build-rn.shthe generated TurboModule sources and native payload
WebAssemblyscripts/package-web-npm.shthe npm tarball (build the wasm package first)

The scripts print their prerequisites when one is missing; they are the same steps the release pipeline runs.

Screenshots

Each capture below comes from the reference application for that platform, on the same recorded Capitol Park ⇔ Tower Bridge trip, in the same state: the turn-by-turn banner with the next maneuver, the planned route polyline with its A and B pins, the ETA-distance line, the playback-speed controls and the exit control. All four were taken from one revision of the SDK without a provider credential stored in the build.

Android — Kotlin and Jetpack Compose

iOS — Swift and SwiftUI

React Native — one TypeScript surface, two native shells

WebAssembly — the browser build

The browser build runs the SDK’s own WebAssembly module and draws through WebGPU, so it is the same core rather than a simulation. The capture shows its consumer surface: the trip planner with both endpoints chosen, the route summary, and the live guidance on the map. It is served keyless at the live demo.

Vector base with place labels

Labels are renderer output, not page markup: the decoder hands the renderer the place and transportation_name features, the style’s symbol layers name the text, and the embedded glyph atlas supplies the shapes. Street names ride their own roads, rotated to the road’s bearing and skipped when the text would not fit; place names sit above them, and a collision pass keeps one from covering another. They arrive with the vector base; a raster base carries its imagery’s own labels instead. Every surface draws them.

Reading the screenshots

The captures share one design language and show the same moment of the same flow: readiness, search, a planned route, and the simulated trip. They also share one vocabulary: maneuver banner, then line, route polyline, map control cluster, compass, scale bar, navigation drawer, and the browser’s trip card. Differences are the platform’s own chrome: Compose’s Material surface on Android, SwiftUI’s safe-area handling on iOS, the React Native host view, and the browser’s WebGPU canvas. The map content, the guidance, the control cluster and the scale ladder are the same.

Versions and support

This page explains how versions are numbered, what a released version line receives, and how to report a problem. The current version is 0.1.0. Requirements and distributions lists the per-platform requirements, and Downloads lists the released artifacts.

Version numbering

Versions follow semantic versioning as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. One workspace version is the single source of truth: the Android, iOS, React Native, and WebAssembly packages are all stamped from it at release time, so one version string identifies one core.

The SDK is pre-1.0. The FFI contract is addition-only, so existing members keep their signature and meaning across an upgrade. Packaging can still change while the release is 0.x: an artifact-set change or a renamed target bumps the minor version, and a pre-1.0 minor can break a build even when the contract did not change. Test a minor upgrade; do not assume it.

Pin exact versions

Release archives are immutable and carry the version in the file name, for example rustic-maps-sdk-android-v0.1.0.aar. Keep the exact version you validated against and upgrade deliberately. The version you pin also names the notices file that accompanies it.

Two release tracks

TrackWhat it isWhat it means for you
StableA vX.Y.Z tag and its release assetsThe version to ship; the support statements on this page apply to it
PreviewA pre-release tag (vX.Y.Z-rc.N) from the same workflow, marked as a pre-releaseEvaluation only; a preview is superseded by the stable release of the same version

Tags are never moved, and a broken release is superseded by a new tag. The failed release’s assets and checksums stay.

Support window

Fixes target the newest minor line; upgrade to it to keep receiving fixes.

Deprecation

The contract’s addition-only rule means a released contract member keeps its signature and meaning; a new release adds members rather than removing them. A deprecation can still mark a member or a packaging detail as superseded. Release notes and the changelog announce it before the release that retires it.

Checking the loaded version

The compiled SDK exposes getSdkCompiledVersion on every surface. Compare it with the artifact you shipped. A mismatch means the loaded core and your dependency declaration disagree, and a diagnostics screen should show the value.

Getting support

Report a problem through the project’s issue tracker with four things: the getSdkCompiledVersion output, your platform and operating system version, the exact SDK version you pinned, and a minimal reproduction. For a rendering problem, include the FrameStatistics of an affected frame. For a provider problem, include the SdkError variant and its detail.

Changelog

The SDK is pre-1.0. Version 0.1.0 artifacts are published on the downloads page; the entries below describe the capabilities they carry. They are grouped by area, with the most recently completed work first.

The FFI contract is addition-only: existing members keep their signature and meaning across an upgrade, so a release adds to the surface rather than rewriting your calls. The versions and support page explains the numbering and the release tracks.

Vector base maps and labels

  • Install any {z}/{x}/{y} vector tileset as a styled base map. Five named styles ship: Bright and Positron (light), Fiord (dark) for OpenMapTiles-schema tilesets, and Carto Light and Carto Dark for the OpenStreetMap US Sourdough tileset. A style can be switched without refetching a tile: decoded geometry is restyled from the tile cache.
  • A styled base replaces the raster tiles while it is installed and draws beneath every overlay, so markers, routes and the location indicator stay on top. The native surface paints the base’s background immediately and fills in tiles as they arrive; the browser resolves a frame’s tiles concurrently rather than one after another.
  • Place names and road names draw from an SDF glyph atlas on every surface. Point-placed names sit at their feature; road names rotate along their own lines. Labels are filtered by feature rank and class, collision-rejected and capped per frame.
  • A status readback reports the configured source and style, the drawn and failed tile counts of the last resolved frame, and the last tile failure detail, so an application can show an honest loading or unavailable state.
  • A Mapbox Vector Tile v2.1 decoder turns fetched tiles into layers, features and geometries, with typed errors on every malformed path.

Positioning

  • The Rust map-positioning crate validates the fixes a device source reports, ignores stationary repeats when averaging course, smooths the course around the circle (so 350° and 10° average to north), tracks staleness and records source failures, so the location indicator, follow camera and navigation controller read one consistent stream.
  • A simulated position source walks a route with course and accuracy for tests, demos and desktop applications before a platform source is wired.
  • The positioning controller and its fix and source-error records are part of the SDK contract, so Kotlin, Swift and TypeScript applications construct the same controller, feed it fixes and read the smoothed course and staleness.
  • The browser demo uses it with the Geolocation API: its Location settings show the device’s position, draw the tracking dot and centre the map, reporting denied, unavailable and timed-out sources honestly. Other hosts supply fixes from their own location API, so permission and lifecycle stay where the operating system requires them.

MapView and the reference applications

  • One MapView per platform owns the map surface, the frame pump, the lifecycle, gestures, the camera, overlays, the location indicator and the listener callbacks. Above it sit MapSdk, Navigator and the small engine objects.
  • Frames are explicit: your display link, choreographer or render pump calls draw with a MapCamera. draw returns the frame’s tile and overlay statistics, and isFrameSettled lets the pump skip a frame when nothing has changed.
  • Overlays are addressed by an identifier the view returns: add, update, remove, replace the whole list, or clear it. A rejected descriptor keeps the previous list in force. Overlay geometry is tessellated once, not rebuilt every frame.
  • The camera is an immutable value with fit-bounds framing, projection and unprojection, and pan, zoom and rotate gestures that hold the point under your finger. The reference applications animate camera presets and frame a route preview with the same insets-aware constructor.
  • The renderer owns the location indicator: a tracking dot with an accuracy ring, or a guided course arrow in navigation follow mode.
  • Android (Compose), iOS (SwiftUI), React Native and the browser reference applications implement one shared design language: a bottom-sheet home, a five-control cluster, a follow camera, an offline tile-cache card, a readiness-chip diagnostics readout, and a Light / Dark / Auto theme whose Auto setting follows the operating system.

Navigation and simulated trips

  • Navigation state is deterministic: the same sequence of location updates produces the same phase, step and instruction. A trip moves through Navigating, OffRoute and Arrived.
  • Step advance supports manual, distance-to-the-end-of-the-step and distance-from-the-step policies. A fix whose reported accuracy is worse than the policy’s minimum never advances.
  • Deviation is graded. A fully-off-route fix freezes progress and asks for a reroute; an off-step-but-on-route fix keeps counting down and reconciles to the projected step.
  • Instruction text is the provider’s own, never rephrased. The instruction payload carries the active maneuver, the next maneuver, a unit-aware distance phrase (immediate, a rounded quantity, or suppressed while progress is frozen), and the roundabout exit index where one applies.
  • The SDK publishes speech triggers over documented distance bands. Each band announces at most once per step, with a minimum spacing and repeat distance to suppress chatter. The platform owns playback and synthesis, and every utterance carries a stable, monotonic identifier.
  • Reroute requests pass through a cooldown and a movement threshold, with an in-flight gate and a readback that says whether a recalculation is running. The defaults are a five-second cooldown and a fifty-meter movement threshold.
  • A subscription delivers one topic: instructions, deviation status, phase changes or speech. A composite subscription delivers all four, and cancel is explicit and idempotent.
  • RouteSimulator interpolates a trip along the planned route’s own polyline at a pace you choose, answers a fix at a travelled distance or an elapsed time, and marks arrival exactly when the fix reaches the final coordinate.

Search, routing and traffic

  • MapSdk resolves every provider-backed call through one registry. The calls cover forward and reverse geocoding, search prediction, full search, routing with ordered waypoints, the distance matrix, traffic incidents, traffic flow and raster tiles. A call into an unregistered contract throws ProviderNotConfigured with the contract name.
  • Route options cover automobile, bicycle and pedestrian modes; fastest and shortest strategies; metric and imperial units; avoiding toll roads, limited-access highways, ferries and unpaved roads; and a departure time.
  • A route carries distance, duration, its bounding box and one leg per waypoint pair, with the maneuver steps inside each leg.
  • SearchEngine, RoutingEngine, OfflineManager and Diagnostics expose the same members as thin facades, so each capability has one object to hold.
  • MapQuest implements the platform API set from one key: geocoding, search prediction, routing, the route matrix, traffic incidents, traffic flow and raster tiles in standard and retina resolutions. Requests share a token-bucket rate limiter, bounded retries for idempotent calls, and a status-to-error mapping.
  • A URL-template provider serves any raster or vector tileset that publishes a {z}/{x}/{y} template, so a base map can come from a platform provider, an OpenStreetMap-based service or your own server without changing a call.
  • Distance matrix and traffic results are available on the native, React Native and WebAssembly surfaces.

Offline maps

  • A deterministic compiler turns an OpenStreetMap PBF extract into a self-describing RMOG routing archive: nodes, a per-edge pack with road class, speed and access columns, and turn restrictions.
  • A validating reader opens the archive from memory-mapped storage or from in-memory bytes. The in-memory path runs in the browser.
  • An offline routing provider answers routes with A* over the graph. It honors recorded turn restrictions and derives turn maneuvers from the bearing change in the geometry, and its instruction text stays honest where the archive carries no street names.
  • When the online provider fails, an offline fallback answers from the graph. An archive that fails validation throws OfflineRoutingFailure.
  • The same graph runs in the browser: the WebAssembly surface loads the compiled archive from in-memory bytes and answers the same route records and refusals as the native targets.
  • Offline tile packs and the disk response cache keep raster imagery available when the network is not. The reference applications include an offline card that plans a route from the bundled archive.

Camera and rendering

  • The SDK draws maps with its own minimal wgpu renderer. It implements web-mercator projection, lists exactly the tiles the camera covers (including across the antimeridian), and draws raster tiles from a byte-bounded GPU texture cache.
  • The tile scheduler deduplicates requests within a frame, falls back to the nearest available parent tile, and respects a per-frame fetch budget. A tile that fails to decode is skipped and evicted so a later frame can refetch it.
  • Route, polygon, marker, pin and traffic-flow overlays draw over the tiles, and the location indicator draws above every overlay.
  • The same renderer draws into live Android and iOS surfaces and on a WebGPU canvas in the browser. High-density surfaces scale labels, line widths and marker radii by the surface’s device pixel ratio, so point sizes stay as designed.
  • The camera math is the SDK’s: platform recognizers forward ordinary screen deltas, and the SDK applies pan, focal-point zoom and focal-point rotation through the camera’s own ranges.

Imagery, providers and caching

  • Raster tiles come from MapQuest or from any {z}/{x}/{y} raster source, in standard or retina resolution. A source is validated when it is registered, so a malformed template or an inverted zoom range refuses immediately.
  • A SQLite-backed response cache holds provider responses under an absolute byte budget, a share of free disk space, or both. It provides per-category time-to-live, LRU eviction, and cache-then-network behavior around every provider contract.
  • Raster tiles cache for 30 days by default, the common ceiling under imagery provider terms. Each provider declares its own ceiling; a requested time-to-live above that ceiling is accepted and clamped, and the effective value, the ceiling and the category default are all readable.
  • The provider surface is vendor-neutral. Ten provider contracts cover geocoding, routing, distance matrix, search, traffic incidents, traffic flow, elevation, raster tiles, offline routing and vector tiles, and a provider is selected by registration rather than by a change to the call.

Provider credentials

  • The SDK needs no provider key at build time. The reference applications start keyless: a URL-template base map draws without a credential, and provider calls answer once a credential is applied.
  • Credentials are entered at runtime from a settings surface whose rows come from one shared provider registry. A key stays in memory unless the user opts in to the device’s secure storage (Keychain on iOS, Keystore on Android).
  • Automated UI runs can inject a credential at launch. It is never persisted or logged.
  • Registering a provider set again replaces every provider slot. Registering a URL-template base map also drops the installed tile cache, because the cache’s terms belong to the provider that installed it, and a fresh cache starts at its category default.

Errors and diagnostics

  • Every failure crosses as one SdkError variant; a variant that carries a detail string carries it verbatim. The reference applications render the same sentence for the same failure across platforms.
  • A diagnostics layer keeps bounded per-subsystem rings. Coordinates are rounded before an event reaches your listener, and only events at or above the severity you subscribe to are delivered.
  • The native and WebAssembly surfaces provide subscribe and flush calls. A flush is bounded, synchronous and non-destructive, so the same event can be read again.
  • A bounded per-object ring records failed calls to a provider you implemented in your own code, classified as a mapped contract error or an unclassified callback failure, with the contract, the method, the time and the verbatim failure text.

Packaging and the live demo

  • A tag-driven release pipeline builds and publishes, when a version tag is pushed:

    • the Android bindings AAR and the MapView wrapper AAR;
    • the iOS XCFramework zip and a generated Swift package manifest;
    • the React Native npm tarball and the WebAssembly npm tarball;
    • the bare WebAssembly archive.

    Each release carries per-asset SHA-256 checksums, an aggregate checksum manifest, Sigstore signature bundles, the third-party notices, the license texts and an install README.

  • The same WebAssembly build powers a keyless live demo. It draws on a WebGPU canvas with pan, zoom, bearing and pitch controls, in-page overlays, recorded route planning, a simulated trip with the SDK’s own navigator, and offline routing from a compiled archive. Its provider panel accepts a runtime key for live geocoding, routing and tile probes.

  • A hosted mobile demo runs the Android, iOS and React Native reference applications on a device.

  • getSdkCompiledVersion answers the loaded core’s version on every surface, so a diagnostics screen can compare it with the artifact you shipped.

Attribution

Each provider descriptor carries its own attribution line and terms note, and the reference applications render the active provider’s line from the shared registry. The keyless demo draws OpenStreetMap data from the OpenFreeMap vector tileset in the Bright style, with the attribution that style requires. Keep the active provider’s attribution visible in your application. Third-party dependency notices are regenerated into Third-party notices.

FAQ and troubleshooting

These are the problems that come up most often when you integrate the SDK, with the check that resolves each. Performance and profiling carries tuning guidance; this page covers failures.

WebGPU and browser support

The browser surface needs WebGPU; there is no WebGL fallback. The wasm canvas fails its initialize() when no WebGPU adapter supports the canvas or the device request fails, and reports the error. Catch it and present a degradation message: name the missing capability (navigator.gpu is the feature test) and link MDN’s compatibility table. The version floor is Chromium 113 flag-free, Safari 26, and Firefox 141 on desktop, always in a secure context (HTTPS or localhost). Do not sniff the user agent.

The map stays empty on an Android emulator after rendering starts. Android emulators render through SwiftShader over ANGLE, a software graphics stack, so this is expected emulator behavior. The GPU surface negotiates through the GL backend: set WGPU_BACKEND=gl in the environment. On real hardware the setting is harmless.

API key and provider failures

How do I supply the provider key? Read it at runtime: from your app’s own secure configuration or a settings screen, and pass it to the provider registration call. Never commit it or bake it into an app bundle. The shipped apps start keyless, take the key from their settings screen, and optionally remember it in the device’s secure store. Automated tests inject a key through a launch value.

The SDK throws immediately at registration when the key is refused. setProviderCredential returns the provider’s detail. Surface it; do not catch and continue.

Calls throw RateLimitExhausted. The shared token-bucket limiter is exhausted. The bucket refills on its own schedule, so retry after the next refill rather than surfacing an error. Cache-then-network behavior around every provider contract keeps repeated identical requests free of quota.

Calls throw ProviderNotConfigured naming a contract. That contract has no registered implementation on the MapSdk object. Registration is per object: re-registration replaces every slot, so a second setProviderCredential call is safe, but a second MapSdk() needs its own registration.

Elevation throws ProviderNotConfigured even with the provider set installed. The shipped providers include no elevation implementation, so elevation calls throw ProviderNotConfigured.

Offline behavior

Tiles render but routes fail offline, or the other way around. The two offline layers are separate. Tile imagery comes from the disk cache you registered with setProviderCredentialWithTileCache, within its byte budget and time-to-live. Routing comes from a compiled routing archive, independent of the imagery cache. Check that the archive covers the queried region.

A route refusal comes back offline. The offline graph refuses rather than guessing in three cases: bytes that fail archive validation, a coordinate outside every node’s snap tolerance, and a request pair the graph cannot connect. Check that the archive covers the areas you query; a small extract is the usual cause.

Maneuver text has no street names offline. The archived graph carries no street-name strings. Offline maneuver text names the turn direction and the distance and states what it does not know. A named maneuver comes from the online provider.

Tile cache

A tuned time-to-live does not stick after re-registration. Registration resets the cache to the category default. Re-apply the override after registering. The rasterTileCacheTerms readback shows the effective value.

A large requested time-to-live is accepted but the cache still expires entries. The installed provider’s declared ceiling, 30 calendar days for the imagery, clamps what the cache retains. Read the ceiling from rasterTileCacheTerms and display it next to the effective value.

Setting a zero time-to-live throws. A zero value would expire every entry on capture. The refusal names the mistake.

Compliance

Attribution. Keep the attribution line visible in your application: imagery © MapQuest; map data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). If you redistribute the SDK or ship an application built on it, reproduce the third-party notices with your distribution.

Third-Party Notices

Generated by scripts/generate-third-party-notices from the workspace dependency graph (Cargo.toml manifests + Cargo.lock, via cargo metadata --offline — no network access). License identities are additionally gated by cargo-deny (deny.toml). Regenerate and commit this file whenever any dependency changes. Output is deterministic, so a re-run on an unchanged graph is a byte-identical no-op.

This file lists the third-party software the workspace depends on: 396 registry packages (338 reachable through normal dependency edges, 58 test/dev-only). The first-party workspace crates are not listed here; they carry the SDK’s own license (MIT OR Apache-2.0, see Cargo.toml).

Separate from the software above: map imagery © MapQuest; map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, licensed under the Open Database License (ODbL). Prior art & inspiration

Credits for projects this SDK learns from. Where only a design was learned from, no code was copied; where an entry says logic was ported, the derived work is credited and its license text is retained under docs/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES/.

  • MapLibre — its open map renderers and how they frame tile scheduling, frustum listing and tile budgeting are the mature prior art this SDK’s renderer seams knowingly re-implement from first principles.
  • OpenStreetMap and its ODbL database — the map-data backbone this SDK renders; the ODbL attribution obligations above are real and are honored in every reference app.
  • UniFFI — whose UDL-first, contract-as-single-source-of-truth binding approach this SDK adopts for its Kotlin/Swift/React Native FFI surface.
  • wgpu — the portable WebGPU-in-Rust stack that lets one GPU rendering path run natively, on mobile, and in the browser.
  • Navara — MapLibre-affiliated web 3D-globe / GIS visualization engine (Rust/WASM headless GIS core); credited as surveyed prior art for headless-engine architecture, not reused and not a reference for this SDK’s navigation capabilities.
  • Ferrostar — Stadia Maps’ Rust navigation core. Its trip-state / step-advance-condition design is the reference this SDK’s map-navigation crate follows closely: the step-advance conditions and their recommended defaults are modeled on Ferrostar’s (including its rapid-double-advance hazard, which this SDK’s ports avoid), and its deviation-detection and spoken-instruction models informed this SDK’s seams. Because this SDK’s navigation logic is derived from Ferrostar’s design, its license text is retained in docs/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES/ferrostar-LICENSE.txt (BSD 3-Clause, Copyright (c) 2023, Stadia Maps, Inc.); no file in this workspace is a verbatim copy, and this SDK’s own code remains MIT OR Apache-2.0.

API reference

The SDK exposes one provider-neutral map platform to five surfaces: Rust libraries, Android/Kotlin, iOS/Swift, React Native and WebAssembly. Every surface carries the same object model, the same records and the same error variants; only the spelling changes with the language.

Use this page to find the right reference page and to learn the rules every surface shares. Each platform page covers every public type that surface exposes: what it does, how it is constructed, every member with its parameters and return value, the failures it can raise, its async and threading rules, and a minimal example.

Choose your surface

SurfaceReferenceYou are writing
RustRust API referencea Rust service, tool or custom target
AndroidAndroid API referenceKotlin or Java on Android
iOSiOS API referenceSwift or SwiftUI on iOS
React NativeReact Native API referenceTypeScript with React Native
WebAssemblyWebAssembly API referenceTypeScript or JavaScript in a browser

The object model

One root object owns provider registration and the tile cache. One surface view draws it. Engines are thin facades over the same root, so a call made through an engine has exactly the same validation, failures and detail messages as the matching root member.

TypePurposeAndroid / iOSReact NativeWebAssemblyRust
MapSdkProvider registry root and async provider callsMapSdkMapsSdk package handle; generated MapSdkMapsSdkProviderRegistry plus the provider traits
MapViewSurface lifecycle, overlays, location layer, vector base, frame statisticsshipped widget plus generated MapViewMapView componentMapView canvas classSurfaceTileRenderer, HeadlessTileRenderer, WorldSpaceOverlayGeometry
MapCameraAnchored camera: center, zoom, bearing, pitchMapCamera plus MapCameraPosegenerated MapCamera; MapCamera pose in the componentMapCameraMapCamera
NavigatorTurn-by-turn trip controllerNavigatorgenerated NavigatorNavigatorNavigationSession and NavigationStateBroadcaster
RouteSimulatorDistance- or time-parameterized trip playbackRouteSimulatorgenerated RouteSimulatorRouteSimulatorRouteWalk
SearchEngineSearch, suggestions and reverse geocodingSearchEnginegenerated SearchEnginefree functionsSearchPlaceProvider, GeocodingProvider
RoutingEngineRoute calculation and distance matrixRoutingEnginegenerated RoutingEnginefree functionsRoutingProvider, DistanceMatrixProvider
OfflineManagerTile-cache terms and time-to-liveOfflineManagergenerated OfflineManagernot exposedmap-core cache policy
DiagnosticsStructured log eventsDiagnosticsgenerated Diagnosticsfree functionstracing events; map-navigation recorder

MapSdk is the only object that holds provider state. Construct it once, register a credential or a base-map source, and pass it to the view and to every engine. Constructing a second root opens a second provider registry and a second tile cache.

Naming across surfaces

ConceptKotlinSwiftTypeScriptRust
TypePascalCasePascalCasePascalCasePascalCase
MembercamelCasecamelCasecamelCasesnake_case
Enum variantUPPER_SNAKE_CASElowerCamelCasePascalCasePascalCase
Record fieldcamelCasecamelCasecamelCasesnake_case
Error typeSdkException sealed classSdkError enumSdkError class with tagSDKError enum

The contract spells record fields in snake_case. Every binding converts them to the language’s own case; the WebAssembly seam does the same for its plain JavaScript objects, so south_west arrives as southWest and maximum_zoom_level as maximumZoomLevel.

Async and threading

  • The provider calls, offlineRouteFromArchiveBytes and MapView.draw are asynchronous. Kotlin uses suspend functions, Swift uses async throws, React Native returns a Promise, WebAssembly returns a Promise. Rust provider traits are async functions through async_trait.
  • Rendering is frame-driven. There is no SDK render thread and no continuous redraw loop. The platform view calls draw once per wanted frame from its own display-link or frame callback, and calls it again only when isFrameSettled answers false.
  • draw holds the view’s render state for its duration. A concurrent draw or resize reports RenderingSurfaceUnavailable; retry the next frame. The shipped Android and iOS views do this automatically.
  • Navigation listener callbacks run synchronously on the thread that drives the controller call. A listener must not block. Calling back into the controller during an in-flight dispatch has its broadcast skipped; the state change behind it is already applied.
  • A listener registered through the diagnostics subscription is called fire-and-forget on the thread that produced the event. A slow listener never slows the event stream.

Failures

Every failing call reports one of these contract variants. Kotlin throws a SdkException subclass, Swift throws the SdkError case, React Native rejects with an SdkError instance and WebAssembly throws the verbatim reason string. The detail string is the verbatim reason and is safe to show to a developer.

VariantMeaning
InvalidCoordinateInputA coordinate, viewport extent, box corner or insets value failed validation.
NetworkRequestFailedThe transport failed: connection, timeout or DNS.
ResponseParsingFailureThe provider answered with a payload the parser cannot use.
ProviderRequestRejectedThe provider returned a documented application-level failure.
RateLimitExhaustedThe token-bucket limiter is exhausted; retry after the next refill.
ProviderNotConfiguredNo provider is registered for the requested contract; the contract name is carried.
InvalidNavigationInputA route record or navigation policy failed validation.
InvalidRenderInputAn overlay, location layer, surface handle or viewport extent is unusable.
RenderingSurfaceUnavailableThe GPU surface is unusable, or the view is busy drawing or resizing.
CacheOperationFailureA cache read, write or eviction failed.
OfflineRoutingFailureAn offline archive is truncated, foreign, unsupported or malformed.

An SDK call never swallows a failure. The shipped Android and iOS map views deliver every failure to their listener or delegate with the wrapper phase it occurred in, keeping the original error as the cause.

Provider registration

Provider credentials never enter source or a build configuration. Read one at runtime and register it on the root; the shipped registration path maps a provider key to that provider’s full contract set. Registering again replaces every slot.

import uniffi.rustic_maps.MapSdk

val mapSdk = MapSdk()
mapSdk.setProviderCredential(credential = providerApiKey)

A base map can also be a provider-neutral {z}/{x}/{y} tileset registered directly on the root, with no provider crate involved. A vector base map is installed on the view with setVectorTileSource and paints one of the SDK’s committed styles.

Where to start

  • Your first map builds a rendered map on every platform.
  • Search and routing drives the engines.
  • Turn-by-turn navigation drives a trip.
  • Offline maps installs a tile cache and routes from an offline graph.

Rust API reference

Generated from the SDK contract and the Rust crate sources. Do not edit this page by hand; change the sources and regenerate the documentation.

The Rust libraries give you the map SDK engine without a platform view: the projection and camera math, the overlay and tile pipeline, provider contracts and their registry, offline routing over compiled archives, and the turn-by-turn navigation core. The same code backs the Android, iOS, React Native and WebAssembly surfaces. This page indexes the public modules and items of the five libraries and carries their documentation comments; the generated Rust documentation carries the full signatures and examples.

Libraries

CrateRole
geospatial_typesShared data records and the error model for the Maps SDK.
geospatial_traitsVendor-neutral provider contracts for the Maps SDK.
map_coreOrchestration core of the Maps SDK: the provider registry, the cache-then-network policy and the typed value boundary between providers and the rest of the SDK.
map_renderingGPU map rendering: camera model, raster tile scheduling with parent fallback and a texture pool, vector-tile styling (fill, line, circle and symbol layers), overlays, and location indicators.
map_navigationTurn-by-turn navigation for a planned route.

Naming and conventions

  • Types are PascalCase, functions and methods are snake_case, and record fields are snake_case.
  • Records are plain Debug + Clone + PartialEq values; none carries a handle or a lock.
  • Provider traits are asynchronous and return Result<_, SDKError>; a provider never panics across the seam.
  • MapCamera and the camera transforms are pure values. Shared state lives behind Arc and short locks.
  • Listener callbacks run on the dispatching thread and must not block; re-entrant dispatch is suppressed by the single-in-flight guard.
  • The GPU renderers are native-only; the WebAssembly target uses the canvas renderer, which shares the camera, scheduler and overlay types.

geospatial_types

Shared data records and the error model for the Maps SDK.

The crate defines the value types exchanged between provider integrations, the rendering engine, the routing engine and the navigation engine: coordinates, bounding boxes, places, route and traffic records, raster and vector tile data, and the unified [SDKError] type.

It performs no input or output and holds no state.

Module vector

Vector tile imagery records.

A vector tile is carried as its wire bytes: the Mapbox Vector Tile (MVT) protobuf, optionally wrapped in gzip by the serving CDN. The record keeps no parsed state, so a cached payload stays byte-identical to what the provider delivered. Parsing into layers and geometries happens in the renderer, not here.

ItemKindSignaturePurpose
VectorTileEncodingenumpub enum VectorTileEncodingWire encoding of a vector tile’s byte payload. Tile services commonly serve MVT protobuf with Content-Encoding: gzip. The record preserves what arrived on the wire; a decoder applies gzip decompression only for [VectorTileEncoding::GzippedMapboxVectorTile].

geospatial_traits

Vendor-neutral provider contracts for the Maps SDK.

The core talks to providers only through the traits in this crate. A vendor integration, an offline engine or a URL-template source implements the relevant traits; no core crate depends on a concrete provider.

Every trait is asynchronous, Send + Sync and object-safe, so an implementation can be shared behind an Arc and registered once at startup. Every method reports failure through [SDKError].

Deterministic mock implementations live in [mock] for use in tests.

Module cache_policy

Cache-then-network orchestration around any provider call.

The caller supplies a [CachedResponseStore] for persistence and a future that performs the network call. Values travel as typed records end to end, so the orchestration path never handles untyped JSON.

ItemKindSignaturePurpose
CacheThenNetworkOutcomeenumpub enum CacheThenNetworkOutcomeWhere a cache-then-network execution took its value from. Callers use this for freshness accounting, such as a staleness indicator in a user interface.
CachedResponseStoretraitpub trait CachedResponseStore<D>: Send + SyncStorage and retrieval of deserialized provider responses, keyed by request fingerprint. D is the typed record the provider returns, for example Vec<PlaceResult>. Implementations must be safe to share across threads.
execute_cache_then_networkfunctionpub async fn execute_cache_then_network<D, FetchFuture>( response_store: &dyn CachedResponseStore<D>, request_fingerprint: &str, time_to_live_seconds: u64, network_fetch: impl FnOnce() -> FetchFuture, ) -> Result<(Arc<D>, CacheThenNetworkOutcome), SDKError>Executes the cache-then-network policy. The store is consulted first. On a hit, the cached value is returned. On a miss, network_fetch is awaited once, the result is stored for time_to_live_seconds, and the fresh value is returned. # Parameters - response_store — the store consulted before and written after the network call. - request_fingerprint — the stable key identifying the request. - time_to_live_seconds — how long the stored value stays valid. - network_fetch — called once, and only on a cache miss. # Returns The value and [CacheThenNetworkOutcome::CacheHit] or [CacheThenNetworkOutcome::NetworkFetch], saying where it came from. # Errors Returns the store’s [SDKError] when the lookup fails, and the network fetch’s [SDKError] when the fetch fails. A failed cache write never fails the call: the fresh value is still returned and storage degrades to cache-less operation. # Async The returned future is safe to poll on any async runtime. The network closure runs after the lookup and before the write.

Module offline_routing

Offline route calculation over compiled routing graph archives.

[ArchiveOfflineRoutingProvider] implements [OfflineRoutingProvider] over a compiled routing graph archive. It loads the archive from a memory-mapped file on native targets or from in-memory bytes on every target, validates it with the archive reader, and builds the adjacency and turn-restriction indexes once. Route requests are then answered with A* under a haversine heuristic.

Targets

The whole module compiles on every target; only graph loading differs.

  • [OfflineGraphSource::Memory] is available everywhere and is the only graph source on WebAssembly. - [OfflineGraphSource::FilePath] memory-maps the archive on native targets. On WebAssembly it returns [SDKError::ProviderRequestRejected] with a message that directs the caller to [OfflineGraphSource::Memory], because the browser has no memory mapping.

Routing behavior

  • Only automobile routing is supported. The archive carries an automobile profile, so a request for another transportation mode is rejected with [SDKError::ProviderRequestRejected] rather than answered. - Costs follow [RouteOptions::route_strategy]: Fastest minimizes edge durations and Shortest minimizes edge distances. Edge speeds and road classes come from each edge record. - Steps are derived from graph metadata. Besides road-class and speed runs, a step boundary occurs at every junction whose signed bearing change leaves the straight band; the step then carries the matching [TurnDirection]. A road-class or speed change without a turn produces a Continue step. The archive carries no street names, so instruction text stays name-free and faithful to the geometry, for example "Turn right" or "U-turn". A strongly curved road yields a step at each junction. - Display and speech text on a step names the maneuver at the step’s end junction, the point a countdown to the next maneuver refers to. [ManeuverType] stays anchored to the maneuver that opens the step. See end_anchored_instruction_text. - Turn restrictions are evaluated against the incoming edge of the settled path. The approximation is exact unless a node is reachable through several best-cost paths with differently restricted incoming edges; in that case it can over-restrict, never under-restrict.

Threading and async

[OfflineRoutingProvider::load_offline_graph] performs its read and validation synchronously inside the async method. It has no await points, so no lock or I/O crosses an await. On WebAssembly, bytes are read and validated in the same synchronous span, with no memory-mapping step. [OfflineRoutingProvider::calculate_offline_route] is pure computation over the loaded graph.

A load validates the new archive completely before replacing the current graph; a failed load leaves the previous graph loaded. The provider is safe to share across threads.

Search engine and performance measurement

[a_star_search] and [dijkstra_reference_search] expose the search engine directly so performance can be measured over the same loaded graph. Dijkstra is a reference baseline only: production routing always goes through A*. Both searches expose [ComputedRoute::settled_node_count], a deterministic expansion metric for comparing them. These items are hidden from generated documentation and are not part of the supported API.

See the module documentation for supported routing behavior, target rules and thread safety.

The bytes are validated by the same reader as [OfflineGraphSource::Memory]. This function is the single implementation behind the corresponding free helper and WebAssembly export, so the native and browser surfaces cannot diverge. # Parameters - archive_bytes — a complete compiled routing graph archive. - start, end — the route endpoints. # Returns A route between the two points, including geometry and steps. # Errors Returns [SDKError::OfflineRoutingFailure] when the archive is truncated, malformed or of an unsupported version. Returns [SDKError::InvalidCoordinateInput] when an endpoint is beyond the graph’s snap tolerance, and [SDKError::ProviderRequestRejected] when the graph cannot connect the two points. Module routing_fallback

Offline route fallback.

[OfflineFallbackRoutingProvider] wraps a primary routing provider and retries a failed request over a configured [OfflineRoutingProvider], joining the per-pair answers into one [RouteData].

Register the wrapper in the registry’s routing slot like any other routing provider. Applications keep using the ordinary [RoutingProvider] contract and need no special handling for offline fallback.

ROUTING_FALLBACK_TRACING_TARGETconstpub const ROUTING_FALLBACK_TRACING_TARGET: &strDiagnostic target of the fallback’s tracing events.
OfflineFallbackRoutingProviderstructpub struct OfflineFallbackRoutingProviderWraps a primary routing provider with an offline retry. When the primary provider fails for a request with at least two waypoints, each consecutive waypoint pair is routed over the loaded offline graph and the answers are joined into one route: one leg per pair, summed distance and duration, and the union bounding box. Behavior: - A successful primary response is returned unchanged, and the offline provider is not consulted. - A request with fewer than two waypoints has no point-to-point offline equivalent, so it is rejected with [SDKError::ProviderRequestRejected] without a fallback attempt. - If the offline retry also fails, that failure is logged and returned. It describes the last failure, matching how a primary failure reaches the caller.

map_rendering

GPU map rendering: camera model, raster tile scheduling with parent fallback and a texture pool, vector-tile styling (fill, line, circle and symbol layers), overlays, and location indicators.

The crate separates scene composition from GPU execution. Projection, camera math, tile scheduling, overlay and label assembly, and the quad assembly in [renderer] are free of wgpu types, so they build and run on every target, including WebAssembly. The native [headless] and [surface] renderers consume that composition and submit it to a wgpu device. On WebAssembly the host page drives WebGPU and consumes the same vertex and style contracts through the wasm bindings.

Module camera

Camera model: geographic center, zoom, bearing, and pitch, projected into a perspective viewport whose ground magnification matches the zoom scale.

The camera uses an anchored perspective model: the ground point under [MapCamera::center] always sits at the viewport center, the camera hovers above it at the altitude implied by the zoom level, and bearing and pitch rotate and tilt the view around that anchor. Projection math runs on f64 matrices because world units reach ~8.6e9 pixels at zoom 24.

The arc also self-limits when the unclamped tightness would dip the zoom past the SDK’s minimum zoom level.

fly_to_animationfunctionpub fn fly_to_animation( start_camera: &MapCamera, target_camera: &MapCamera, viewport: &ViewportPixels, fly_to_options: FlyToOptions, ) -> Result<CameraAnimation, String>The camera animation that flies between two cameras instead of cutting between them: zoom follows the fly-to arc’s exponential dip — long travels zoom out along the way and zoom back in on arrival, short travels slide almost monotonically — while the center, bearing, and pitch ease normally. The arc follows the standard fly-to derivation, adapted to the SDK’s mercator-anchored camera: the visible span w(s) shrinks and grows hyperbolically along the path in units of the initial viewport span, and the derived duration (absent an override) is the arc length over the travel speed. The outer easing stays the SDK’s smoothstep (interpolate_camera uses the same), so both pose curves share one easing story rather than the usual cubic-bezier easing. Use [CameraAnimation::new] for a plain cut-interpolated animation. # Parameters - start_camera — the pose the animation begins at. - target_camera — the pose the animation ends at. - viewport — the viewport the animation is evaluated against. - fly_to_options — the zoom ceiling, arc tightness, travel speed and optional duration override. # Errors Returns a description of the unusable input when a zoom level, the viewport extent, the zoom-out curve or the travel speed is not finite (or not positive where required).
CameraAnimationstructpub struct CameraAnimationTime-driven camera transition between two cameras.
fit_boundsfunctionpub fn fit_bounds( bounding_box: &BoundingBox, viewport: &ViewportPixels, edge_insets: EdgeInsetsPixels, maximum_zoom_level: f64, ) -> Result<MapCamera, String>The camera that frames a bounding box inside the viewport’s inset region. Bounds fitting is top-down and north-up by construction (pitch and bearing zero), matching every leading SDK: perspective fitting is ill-defined and would double-fit against the frustum clip. The zoom is the largest level whose ground scale keeps the whole box inside the inset area, clamped to maximum_zoom_level; the center is the box’s normalized-world midpoint, shifted so its ground point lands on the inset region’s center under asymmetric insets. The whole-box-inside-the-inset-area guarantee holds only for the unclamped fit: when the zoom is clamped (by maximum_zoom_level, or by the minimum zoom for boxes too large for the world), the box overflows the inset region and the center-anchor guarantee is the one that survives. # Parameters - bounding_box — the geographic box to frame. - viewport — the viewport to frame it in. - edge_insets — screen regions kept clear of map content. - maximum_zoom_level — the zoom ceiling for the fit. # Errors Returns a description of the unusable input when the insets or the maximum zoom are not finite, when the insets are negative or leave no inset area (left + right ≥ viewport width and likewise vertical), or when the box spans no positive world area (non-finite or reversed corners).

Module camera_interaction

Camera adjustments driven by platform gesture input.

A platform recognizes gestures (pointer capture, momentum, pinch to zoom, and so on) and forwards plain deltas; [CameraInteraction] owns the camera adjustment those deltas imply. Gesture recognition itself, delta shaping (for example wheel ticks to zoom levels), inertia after a gesture ends, and any zoom-range policy beyond the camera’s own clamp stay on the platform side.

Each method takes the current camera in and returns the adjusted camera, so the caller keeps single ownership of the live pose. The methods reuse the anchored camera’s clamping and projection math rather than duplicating it.

The focal-point correction is exact, not iterative: a screen pixel’s ground ray direction depends only on bearing, pitch, field of view and viewport — never on zoom or camera position — so after a zoom or rotate delta, translating the camera anchor by the ground offset between where the candidate camera projects the focal pixel and the held ground point puts the world point back under the focal pixel at any pitch.

ItemKindSignaturePurpose
CameraInteractiontraitpub trait CameraInteractionGesture-delta camera adjustments. Every method takes the pose in, answers the resulting pose out, and never mutates: [MapCamera] is small and Copy, so callers keep single ownership of the live pose while applying deltas. Pan, focal zoom and rotation are the supported deltas; the camera’s own clamps (zoom [0, 24], pitch [0, 75]°, bearing wrapped into [0, 360)) and Mercator latitude bounds always hold on the answer.

Module gpu_texture_cache

Byte-bounded LRU cache of tiles already uploaded to GPU memory.

Uploads are expensive — every pooled payload is decoded to its full RGBA8 image and copied onto the device — and a steady camera keeps the same tiles visible for many consecutive frames. This cache stores what [crate::headless::HeadlessTileRenderer] uploaded, keyed by tile and stamped with the pool’s payload revision (see [crate::tile_texture_pool::TileTexturePool::payload_revision]): a pool insert under the same key replaces the bytes, so a cached texture whose revision no longer matches is stale and must never be drawn from. Frames prune stale entries first, then draw from whatever survives.

Eviction order is least-recently-used, and the budget is a mirror of the encoded-payload pool’s byte budget idea: as with the pool, a single oversized texture is kept alone rather than flash the map.

ItemKindSignaturePurpose
GPU_TILE_TEXTURE_CACHE_DEFAULT_MAXIMUM_BYTESconstpub const GPU_TILE_TEXTURE_CACHE_DEFAULT_MAXIMUM_BYTES: u64Default GPU byte budget, sized as a heuristic for one complete 16 × 16 tile grid of 256-px RGBA8 tiles — the payload size platform raster tile sources typically produce. Budgets size the cache, not the textures: the upload path textures whatever a payload decodes to, so a 512-px payload holds half as many tiles in the same byte budget.
GpuTileTextureCachestructpub struct GpuTileTextureCacheLRU cache of uploaded tile textures, bounded in GPU bytes.

Module headless

Headless wgpu rendering of raster tiles plus deterministic frame capture.

The renderer draws one textured quad per pooled tile for a single frame into an off-screen render-attachment texture and reads the pixels back into a [CapturedFrame]; an optional overlay layer ([crate::overlay::MapOverlay]) draws after the quads in the same render pass through a separate solid-color pipeline. Pooled payloads that fail to decode are skipped for the frame and evicted from the pool so the scheduler refetches them: one corrupt tile never poisons the frames after it. Only structural failures (an overflowing draw list, a failed context acquisition or capture) are errors. No window surface is requested, so this works on any native backend (Metal, Vulkan, DirectX). Device acquisition lives behind the object-safe [GraphicsContextSource] trait, which keeps wgpu types out of the scheduling core and lets a caller substitute its own context source or skip rendering when no adapter exists.

This module is native-only: it blocks on the asynchronous wgpu initialization calls and polls the device, which is not valid on WebAssembly, where the browser’s own async runtime drives WebGPU.

Capturing snapshots

A capture composes the scene into an off-screen render attachment that is never presented to a window, and [capture_frame_bytes] reads the result back. The readback is inherently blocking ([capture_frame_bytes] escalates to a blocking device poll).

For deterministic captures, [HeadlessTileRenderer::snapshot_frame_when_idle] refuses to render while pending tile work remains, returning [HeadlessRenderError::PendingTileWork] immediately without touching the GPU; otherwise it behaves exactly like the ordinary capture. The refusal decision costs no device work and never waits for pending work to finish. Completing that work is the caller’s next prepare frame. [HeadlessTileRenderer::render_captured_frame_with_overlays] is the ungated form: it always renders and captures, however much tile work is still pending.

The idle gate covers tile fetch state only; camera animations are composed outside this renderer entirely (see [crate::tile_scheduler] on the full idle semantics).

Module labels

The frame-level label pass: symbol-layer text from decoded vector tiles becomes screen-space glyph quads, anchored at a point for place and POI names and run along a line for road names.

The pass is deliberately GPU-free, like the overlay assembly: the native headless renderer, the native surface and the browser canvas all call the same functions and upload the same vertices, so the backends cannot drift in where a label lands or which labels survive.

Three stages:

  1. [label_candidates_for_vector_tile] walks a decoded tile’s symbol-layer features and reads each label’s text through the style’s ordered fallbacks. Candidates keep the style’s paint, size, priority, rank, placement and overlap rule. A symbol layer also filters before a feature becomes a candidate: its rank must pass the layer’s zoom-stepped rank ceiling, and its class must be useful at the frame’s zoom (a shop waits until the layer’s per-class minimum zoom). A [VectorSymbolPlacement::Point] layer anchors a candidate at each of the feature’s points; a [VectorSymbolPlacement::Line] layer carries the feature’s whole line geometry so the frame can place the text along it. 2. [LabelLayer::place] projects the candidates through the frame camera, sorts them by priority, then style order, then rank (the documented collision-priority rule: lower priority is more important), and greedily rejects any label whose padded screen rectangle intersects a label already placed. allow_overlap labels skip the test and never block later labels. The frame places at most [MAXIMUM_LABELS_PER_FRAME] labels: once that budget is spent, every remaining candidate is dropped even if it would fit, so a dense downtown cannot out-shout the places that matter. A label whose text repeats an already-placed label is dropped, so the buffered overlap between adjacent tiles cannot paint one place twice. The output order is a pure function of the input order and the camera.

A line-placed label projects its geometry and takes its longest straight run (consecutive near-collinear segments) as the text’s run: the text is centered halfway along that run, rotated to its chord bearing, flipped so it always reads upright, and skipped when the run is shorter than the text plus the collision padding at each end. The collision rectangle is the axis-aligned box around the rotated text, so it rejects exactly like a point label’s. 3. [LabelLayer::quad_vertices] lays the glyph bitmaps out on the atlas and emits clip-space textured quads, halo first and text second. A rotated label rotates each glyph’s screen-space rectangle about the label’s anchor before converting it to clip space, so every backend that draws these vertices carries rotation without a second vertex format.

Latin text is measured from the decoded glyph ranges and nothing here shapes complex scripts (see map-glyphs). A frame with no symbol layers or no glyphs produces no vertices, so the tiles-only pipelines stay byte-identical.

ItemKindSignaturePurpose

Noto Sans’ ascender at that size is 26 pixels (the payload’s no-ink space glyph stores -26).

GLYPH_TEXT_SIGNED_DISTANCE_THRESHOLDconstpub const GLYPH_TEXT_SIGNED_DISTANCE_THRESHOLD: f32The signed-distance value at which a glyph bitmap counts as covered. The glyph protocol is node-fontnik’s encoding, byte = 255 - (64 + 32 × distance_px), so the zero-distance contour — the glyph outline — sits at (256 − 64)/256 = 0.75, not at 0.5. Thresholding at 0.5 dilates every glyph by (0.75 − 0.5) × 8 = 2 atlas pixels per side, which closes counters and fattens strokes. Thresholding at 0.75 keeps the outline faithful to the font.

GLYPH_SIGNED_DISTANCE_FIELD_MAXIMUM_OUTWARD_PIXELSconstpub const GLYPH_SIGNED_DISTANCE_FIELD_MAXIMUM_OUTWARD_PIXELS: f64The glyph protocol’s border, in atlas pixels: the distance field fades to zero beyond this many pixels outside the ink box, so a halo can only reach this far before it samples the border texel.

The drawn text size in device pixels is the same number times the device pixel ratio; the two uses keep the band at 0.84 device pixels at every size and ratio.

The packed atlas rides in an [Arc], so handing the font to [LabelLayer::place] never re-copies the page, and the renderer’s atlas upload happens once per distinct revision. The embedded bytes are part of the library; should they ever fail to decode or pack (a corrupted build rather than a normal path), the in-code fallback is an empty font stack: every label measures no glyph and the pass paints nothing, so a map still draws instead of failing. A feature becomes a candidate only when its rank passes the layer’s zoom-stepped rank ceiling and its class is visible at style_zoom_level under the layer’s per-class minimum zooms, so a busy poi layer draws its important places at a wide zoom and its shops only once the map is closer. A point-placed symbol layer then produces one candidate per feature point; a line-placed one produces one candidate carrying each feature’s line geometry, which the frame places along its longest projected segment. Features of a geometry kind the placement cannot use paint nothing for that symbol layer, exactly like the overlay conversion.

Module location_indicator

GPU-free location-indicator assembly: the position fix drawn as a screen-facing disc with its optional ground-projected accuracy ring and a course-directed wing, in the same clip-space stream pattern the overlay layer uses (see [crate::overlay]).

The indicator is the third draw layer of a frame — the explicit draw order is tiles, then overlays, then the indicator ([LOCATION_INDICATOR_TOP_LAYER_DRAW_ORDER]) — so the fix’s visuals always paint over route lines and polygons without the overlay list growing or reordering. The vertices reuse the [crate::overlay::ClipSpaceOverlayVertex] type and draw through the existing overlay solid-color pipeline (a shader/layout-identical third pass), alpha-blended over what the first two layers drew.

Layer semantics:

  • Screen anchoring. The disc and its wing are screen-space shapes anchored at the fix’s projected position — the fix’s pixel stays fixed under zoom and pan while the layers beneath move, exactly like point markers do (center anchoring, “screen-facing”). At pitch this keeps the dot legible where a ground-projected dot would foreshorten to a sliver, and the wing rotates with the camera’s bearing so a course heading reads as the same compass direction it reads on the ground. * The guided-course visual. [LocationIndicatorVisualKind::GuidedCourseArrow] draws the course wing — a cone of [HEADING_WEDGE_HALF_ANGLE_DEGREES] half-angle reaching [LOCATION_COURSE_WEDGE_REACH_PIXELS] up-course from the disc center — underneath the same disc the plain form draws; with the course unknown (None) it degrades to the plain dot. The visual is a disc with a course cone, not a separate arrow sprite. * Accuracy ring. A ground-projected circle of the fix’s horizontal accuracy — the honest reading of “this fix is this accurate” — drawn through the filled-polygon machinery, so it foreshortens into the ellipse the ground shows at pitch and splits at world-copy boundaries like every other ground shape. A fix more accurate than [MINIMUM_ACCURACY_RING_DRAW_METERS] draws no ring (a circle inside the disc itself carries no information), and an absurdly coarse fix clamps to [MAXIMUM_ACCURACY_RING_DIAMETER_PIXELS] on screen instead of flooding the viewport. * World copies. The screen-facing shapes anchor once per visible world-copy window like the tile spans’ fragments, so at the zoom < 1 world-copy views the indicator draws in every copy that renders the fix; the ground ring splits across windows in the polygon machinery. * Behind the camera. A screen-shape anchor whose homogeneous weight is not positive (the fix behind the camera plane) draws no disc or wing — the screen-space shapes’ documented skip — while the ground-projected ring still projects by genuine corners and leaves near-plane straddling to the GPU’s frustum clip.

Module overlay

GPU-free overlay assembly: route polylines, filled polygons, point markers, and traffic-flow lines projected into clip-space solid-color triangle lists drawn over the tile quads.

Overlays are the second draw layer of a captured frame: the same camera pose and viewport that assemble the tile quads ([crate::renderer::Renderer::frame_quads]) also project overlay shapes into clip-space triangles via [overlay_triangle_vertices], which the headless renderer draws through a separate solid-color pipeline in the same render pass after the tiles. The WebAssembly canvas mirrors the vertex contract verbatim, so the assembly here is deliberately wgpu-free and emits one flat, non-indexed triangle list.

Assembly semantics:

  • World copies / antimeridian. Overlay geometry wraps around the camera exactly like tile spans do (see [crate::renderer::FrameProjection]): the first vertex of a shape sits in the camera’s world copy via the shortest wrapped delta, every following vertex unwraps continuously from it, and each resulting segment or triangle is split against the camera-centered world-copy windows ([WORLD_COPY_WINDOW_OFFSETS], reusing the tile spans’ window half-width). A shape wider than the covered window range clips to nothing beyond it; a single unwrapping step never spans more than half a world, so three windows cover every reachable fragment. * Frustum clipping. Assembly relies on the GPU’s clip-space frustum clip, the same mechanism the tile pipeline relies on for near-plane straddling spans; no extra CPU cull runs. Screen-space-thickened shapes (route lines, markers, traffic) additionally drop the segments and markers with a vertex at or behind the camera because the screen-space width offset needs a positive homogeneous weight; filled polygons emit genuine clip-space corners and keep near-plane straddling triangles for the GPU to clip exactly. * Line joins. A polyline draws as butt-capped segment quads plus one screen-space square (the line’s width) per interior vertex, oriented along the bend’s bisector. The square fills the wedge the butt caps leave outside a bend, which otherwise reads as a gap between styled road segments; it never grows a miter spike at sharp angles. Endpoints keep their butt caps (a per-feature end has no neighbouring segment to join), and sharp joins can still show a sliver where the wedge exceeds the square; a full round-join fan would close that gap. * Polygon holes. A filled polygon carries one outer ring and any number of hole rings. Holes join the outer boundary through the standard bridge-splicing step before ear clipping ([FilledPolygonOverlay] documents the algorithm), so the emitted triangle stream covers exactly the ring set’s even-odd interior: the overlay pipeline paints a flat triangle list with alpha blending and has no stencil test, so a hole must leave its region out of that list rather than erase it after the fact. * Markers. A marker is a regular-octagon triangle fan centered on the projected anchor point (center anchoring, not bottom pinning): the projected coordinate is the fan’s center, so a marker’s center sits exactly at its geographic position. Sprites and label callouts are drawn by other layers. * Pins. A pin is a teardrop anchored the other way: its tip sits on the projected coordinate and the circular head above it carries a hollow center. The teardrop is star-shaped around the head center, so the outline is one radial function of the angle and the hollow center is the annulus between that outline and an inner circle — again a plain triangle list, no erase pass.

Screen-space line widths, joins, marker radii and pin outlines are authored as per-vertex pixel parameters and expanded in the vertex shader, so they still follow the CPU assembly’s screen-pixel math exactly while the tessellation stays camera-free. World-copy handling moves to the frame path too: the shader recenters each vertex by the drawn instance’s copy offset and discards fragments outside the camera’s own world-copy window, reproducing the CPU assembly’s window split and antimeridian wrap without re-tessellating.

Module prefetch

GPU-free predictive prefetch planning: the bounded tile set a caller warms ahead of motion so the pool covers the camera’s next poses.

The planner emits an ordered request list — the camera’s visible set at its tile zoom first, then the ring of tiles ahead along the bearing vector ([PREFETCH_RING_TILES] viewport-heights ahead), then a navigation route corridor’s tiles when navigation feeds one, then one coarser fallback zoom under everything ([PREFETCH_FALLBACK_ZOOM_BELOW] below the camera’s tile zoom) — deduplicated against the pool’s contents and an already-warming set, capped at [PREFETCH_MAXIMUM_CONCURRENT_FETCHES]. The list feeds [crate::tile_scheduler::TileScheduler::warm_tiles] or its detached [crate::tile_scheduler::TileScheduler::plan_warm_tiles] twin, whose own per-call budget keeps the concurrent fetches bounded.

The navigation-corridor entries keep exactly the road corridor warm, and the effect is visible through the frame statistics a caller collects.

Module projection

Web-mercator projection: geographic coordinates, normalized world space, and the XYZ tile grid.

Normalized world coordinates span [0, 1] in both axes — x grows eastward from the antimeridian, y grows southward from the north pole — so a single multiplication by [zoom_scale_pixels] places geometry in screen-scale units. All math stays in f64 because world units reach ~8.6e9 pixels at zoom 24, beyond f32 mantissa precision.

Module renderer

GPU-free frame assembly: prepared tiles mapped to drawable quads.

The pure half of the renderer. A [Renderer] consumes the camera pose, the viewport, and the tiles the [crate::tile_scheduler::TileScheduler] prepared for the frame, and produces the list of textured quads to draw in normalized world coordinates, including parent-fallback quads for tiles that are not yet pooled.

Quads are projected into per-fragment clip-space vertex arrays: a world span is wrapped around the camera as one unit (never corner by corner) and split into at most one vertex array per world copy it reaches, so spans crossing the antimeridian render contiguously instead of tearing. See [FrameProjection].

Everything in this module is free of wgpu types, so the quad assembly, the fallback texture window math, and the clip-space projection of the quad corners are all unit-testable without a GPU.

Module surface

Surface rendering of raster tiles plus overlays onto a live native window: the same scene composition as the headless renderer, presented through a real wgpu::Surface.

The renderer draws one textured quad per pooled tile for a single frame and an optional overlay layer ([crate::overlay::MapOverlay]) after the quads in the same render pass — byte-for-byte the headless pipeline’s geometry and shaders (the private shader sources and encode helpers mirror [crate::headless], and the WebAssembly canvas follows the same pattern) — but the frame renders into the next acquired surface texture and is presented, not captured. The pipelines therefore target the surface’s negotiated format (for example Bgra8Unorm under Metal), unlike the headless capture’s fixed FRAME_TEXTURE_FORMAT; the negotiation happens once at construction from the documented preference list and every later configuration keeps it.

Lifecycle

Per-platform raw window handles lower into a [wgpu::SurfaceTargetUnsafe] outside this crate, which takes over from there — this module is platform-agnostic and never names a windowing backend:

  1. Wrap the unsafe target with [SurfaceRenderTarget::from_unsafe_target], which creates the wgpu::Instance and the 'static [wgpu::Surface] against it. The raw handle must stay valid for the surface’s whole lifetime; wgpu’s own validity rules apply (see [wgpu::SurfaceTargetUnsafe]). 2. Build the renderer with [SurfaceTileRenderer::new], acquiring the adapter/device/queue through the injected [SurfaceGraphicsContextSource] (production: [WgpuSurfaceGraphicsContextSource], which requests an adapter compatible with the surface, unlike the headless source). The surface format is negotiated here. 3. Size the render area explicitly with [SurfaceTileRenderer::configure_extent] — resize is a call, not an observation: only a configure changes the swap-chain extent. A zero extent is refused; an already-configured extent reconfigures only when the extent changes. 4. Draw every frame with [SurfaceTileRenderer::render_frame]; the frame’s viewport must match the configured extent exactly. A stale surface (window resized or torn down behind the renderer’s back) reconfigures once and retries the acquisition before failing. 5. Detach by dropping the renderer: the wgpu surface’s own release semantics are its drop behavior (wgpu 30 has no separate un-configure call), so the host’s surface view drops the renderer — and every [SurfaceRenderTarget] it wraps — when its window handle goes away.

Attaching and detaching the underlying platform view belong to the caller. Dropping the [SurfaceRenderTarget] while its raw handle is reused elsewhere is a caller error to avoid, so the host code that owns the view must outlive the renderer.

Native only

Like [crate::headless], this module blocks on the asynchronous wgpu initialization and configuration calls (pollster) and is not valid on WebAssembly, where the browser runtime drives WebGPU.

Module tile_scheduler

Frame-driven raster tile scheduling with parent fallback.

Each frame the scheduler receives the XYZ tiles the camera needs (usually from [crate::projection::tiles_covering] on the camera footprint). For every requested tile it reports one readiness:

  • Present — pooled at the requested zoom; * FallsBackTo — a nearest pooled ancestor stands in while the detailed tile loads or while its fetch failed, so the map blurs instead of flashing holes; * Unavailable — the provider rejected the tile this frame; a later frame may retry.

Fetches are deduplicated within a frame (one provider call per distinct tile), ordered most-detailed-first, and capped by the configured per-frame fetch budget; requests beyond the cap report Deferred.

The idle render-state signal

An idle state means no more tile loads remain, so a capture made then cannot race a late fetch. This module exposes render-state queries: [TileScheduler::is_idle] over the fetch state, and [prepared_frame_is_idle] over a captured frame’s readiness verdicts.

What counts as pending is stated over the fetch state, because the scheduler itself is frame-driven: [TileScheduler::prepare_frame] awaits every fetch it issues, so a fetch is never observable through this API mid-flight. The pending states are therefore exactly the readiness verdicts whose pixels a later successful frame can still change:

  • Deferred — the fetch budget spent; a later frame fetches the tile. * Unavailable — the provider rejected the tile; a later frame retries it. * FallsBackTo — a coarser ancestor covers the area while the detailed tile loads or its fetch failed; when the fetch lands, the area re-renders at its own detail level.

A frame is idle when every requested tile resolved Present: no scheduled work can change its pixels. An empty request set is idle by vacuity. Idle is a query, not an event: it can flip back to pending when the pool loses a requested payload — least-recently-used budget pressure, or the renderer evicting an undecodable payload after a draw — until the next prepare frame refetches it.

Explicitly not part of the verdict: camera animations (crate::camera::CameraAnimation), which are composed entirely outside the renderer; GPU upload state, which never spans calls on the headless render path because uploads happen synchronously inside one frame render (the WebAssembly canvas, in contrast, keeps browser fetches in flight across a render frame); and evictions of payloads the current request set does not ask for.

Synchronous resolve and detached warm fetches

The frame path never awaits the network: [TileScheduler::resolve_frame] answers every requested tile’s readiness from the pool’s current state alone (plus the in-flight warming set it reports as Deferred), purely synchronously, and the misses are fetched by [TileScheduler::warm_tiles] (or its detached twin [TileScheduler::plan_warm_tiles], whose [TileWarmTask] runs on the caller’s background runtime) so detail arrives in a later frame. The blocking [TileScheduler::prepare_frame] awaits every fetch it issues; both paths report the same readiness verdicts over the same pool.

Diagnostics emit per-frame resolve and warm events at the Debug level and per-tile fetch events at the Trace level under the tile_fetch target, behind the diagnostics severity gate.

The two forms agree for a frame checked immediately after the prepare_frame that produced it; they can diverge only if the pool changed in between — an eviction leaves the recorded verdicts resolved while is_idle reports pending again. The verdict form is exactly the gate a deterministic capture needs at capture time; the pool form is what a caller re-checks before a later frame.

Module vector_base

Shared vector-tile base pipeline: one scheduler that fetches a vector tileset through the [VectorTileProvider] trait, decodes each tile once, styles it, and answers the overlay primitives the frame draws beneath its own overlays.

Every target serves its vector base through this one implementation, so the native surfaces and the browser cannot drift in what a tile paints. The scheduler owns two caches:

  • Decoded tiles, keyed by the tile address: a tile’s bytes are fetched and decoded once and never again while it stays cached; a style change restyles the decoded tile instead of refetching it. - Styled geometry, keyed by the tile address, the style revision and the style’s zoom bucket: the style’s zoom span (min_zoom/max_zoom) and width stops are evaluated at the camera’s zoom level, so a camera pan across a width stop repaints the tile from the style it already carries — no refetch, no decode. The zoom level quantizes to [VECTOR_BASE_STYLE_ZOOM_QUANTIZATION_STEPS_PER_LEVEL] steps per level so a continuous zoom gesture cannot grow the styled cache without bound.

A tile that fails to fetch or decode does not fail the frame: the scheduler skips it, keeps painting the tiles that succeeded, and reports the failure in the frame’s counts and its last failure detail. The base map is one layer of a frame, never the frame’s reason to fail.

The scheduler is camera-agnostic: the caller lists the visible tile addresses (through MapCamera::visible_tile_keys or the page’s own grid) and names the camera’s zoom level; [VectorBaseScheduler::served_zoom_level] clamps that listing to the tileset’s declared zoom span.

Each resolved frame also carries the drawn tiles’ label candidates, read from the active style’s symbol layers. [VectorBaseFrame::label_layer] places them at a camera pose through the SDK’s embedded default glyph font, so every platform surface draws the same place names without a platform-specific asset. A frame without candidates yields None and costs the renderer nothing.

A 1080p frame asks for a few dozen tiles, so the cache holds several camera positions’ worth of decoded geometry: a pan back over visited ground repaints without refetching.
